speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will still have the formal Second Reading of the CPF (Amendment) Bill to ensure that procedural requirements are dealt with.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore’s labour market is adapting to an older workforce, in tandem with demographic needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the support of the tripartite partners, between 2010 and 2019, we have made necessary adjustments to our employment and retirement policies, so that senior workers can continue to work beyond 65 if they wish.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We started promoting the concept of re-employment in 2007 and, after extensive outreach, established the re-employment age to be 65 in 2012.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We then raised the re-employment age to 67 in 2017.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These innovations in our labour market have helped allow our seniors to remain economically active.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By 2020, about a quarter of our resident labour force was aged 55 and above.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is up from 16.5% a decade ago.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This has helped more of our senior workers earn more and save more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With CPF LIFE, they have added assurance of a perpetual monthly income in their retirement years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In 2018, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) called for a fresh effort to prepare Singapore's ageing workforce for the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In response, we formed the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers (the Workgroup) to: one, review the longer-term relevance of the retirement age and re-employment age and consider our next moves; two, to examine the CPF contribution rates for senior workers and their impact on retirement adequacy; and three, to promote an inclusive workforce and progressive workplaces that value senior workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Workgroup consulted extensively and presented its recommendations to the Government in 2019.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One of its key recommendations was to retain the statutory retirement and re-employment age framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Under this framework, employers cannot terminate an employee on grounds of age before the statutory retirement age.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Workers have the assurance of continued employment up till the statutory re-employment age if they are able and if they wish to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, businesses have sufficient flexibility to adjust re-employment terms, enabling them to continue providing employment opportunities to our senior workers while remaining competitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It was also observed from other countries' experiences that doing away with the statutory ages does not necessarily lead to higher employment rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Workgroup had assessed this to be a realistic goal, considering improvements in health and life expectancy, the better-educated and higher-skilled workers today, as well as enhanced organisational capabilities and capacity to manage our senior workers well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Achieving this by the end of this decade also provides time for employers to adjust.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Another key recommendation of the Workgroup was to raise the CPF contribution rates for workers aged 55 to 70 over the next decade, to boost retirement adequacy for our seniors, even as we provide them with the flexibility to continue working for longer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The increases are to be phased in gradually, taking into account prevailing economic conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When completely implemented, the full CPF contribution rates will apply to senior workers up to age 60, compared to 55 today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The rates will step down gradually for workers above 60.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, the Workgroup recommended that employers undertake complementary changes to their policies, processes and practices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers should engage mature and senior workers in structured career planning sessions at certain age milestones to plan their future career trajectories as well as training requirements.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To encourage more age-friendly workplaces, employers should also embark on job-redesign, as well as provide more part-time re-employment opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Bill today amends the Retirement and Re-employment Act to establish the maximum possible statutory retirement and re-employment ages at 65 and 70 respectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This reflects the recommendations of the Tripartite Workgroup.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The prevailing retirement and re-employment ages will continue to be prescribed by notification in the Gazette.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will be effective from 1 July 2022, that is, next year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Naturally, employers who wish to move faster are free to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, the public sector has already taken the lead, by implementing a retirement age of 63 and a re-employment age of 68 one year earlier on 1 July this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Other recommendations of the Workgroup are also being implemented.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employees aged 55 to 70 will see an increase in total CPF contribution rates of up to two percentage points.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This increase was deferred by a year from the original announced timeline of 1 January 2021 as a nimble move to help employers manage costs amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The deferment was also supported by the Labour Movement which viewed this as a balanced approach to help senior workers keep their jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our ability to shift gears and to jointly focus on tackling the immediate challenges at hand while not losing sight of our longer-term vision, is a true reflection of the strength of Singapore's tripartism model.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to engage our tripartite partners at each phase of rate increases over this decade.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are also grants to encourage employers to go one step further and raise their internal retirement and re-employment ages above the statutory ages, and to provide more part-time work options for senior workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those who do not wish to continue working need not do so and can enjoy their retirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To be clear, these changes will not affect existing CPF withdrawal policies and ages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At age 55, you can still withdraw at least $5,000 and you can still start your CPF payouts from age 65 onwards.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Bill makes various amendments to simplify the CPF system for members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we will make it easier for members to receive retirement payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For members who receive payouts through the Retirement Sum Scheme, some have fully drawn down their Retirement Account but still have funds in their Ordinary or Special Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will automatically draw down from these accounts to continue providing them a monthly payout.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For members who receive payouts through CPF LIFE, some have subsequent inflows into their Retirement Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will convert them into higher CPF LIFE payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For members turning 65 from 2023, we will give them greater flexibility to decide on when their Ordinary or Special Account savings will be transferred into their Retirement Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are over 250,000 members currently receiving payouts under the Retirement Sum Scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are members who had not opted into CPF LIFE.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Under the Retirement Sum Scheme, members stop receiving payouts once their Retirement Account is depleted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, many members still have funds in their Ordinary or Special Account, the OSA accounts, because they continue to receive CPF inflows, such as contributions from employment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some members are not aware that they can transfer these funds into their Retirement Account and continue to receive a monthly payout.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With this amendment, we will make it easier for them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: John has been receiving monthly Retirement Sum Scheme payouts of $700.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He has now completely depleted his Retirement Account, but he still has $2,500 in his Ordinary and Special Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Under current rules, this $2,500 will remain in his Ordinary and Special Account unless he comes forward to withdraw it or apply to transfer it to his Retirement Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With this amendment, John will continue to receive his monthly payout of $700 automatically, drawing from his Ordinary and Special Account savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: After the $2,100 has been paid out in three tranches – remember that John has $2,500 in his Ordinary and Special Account – the remaining $400 in John's Ordinary and Special Account will be disbursed to him as the final payout.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If John is still working, the continued contributions to his Ordinary and Special Account will allow him to receive payouts for longer and fuss-free.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: John will receive the payouts when his CPF savings have accumulated to at least $250, or at least once a year if less than $250.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: John can also approach CPF Board or visit the CPF website to check how he can withdraw the remaining amount.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: About 75,000 members are currently receiving CPF LIFE payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For subsequent inflows into their Retirement Account, members currently need to apply to add these inflows to their LIFE payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Again, we will automate this process by this month, making it easier for members to enjoy the higher payouts for life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These changes will make it easier for members to tap on their CPF savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is worth mentioning that besides CPF, many of our seniors have access to other assets, such as housing, private savings and investments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For seniors who had low incomes during their working years and now have less in their retirement, the Silver Support Scheme was recently enhanced to broaden the eligibility criteria and to increase the quarterly cash payouts by 20%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, members already have some flexibility over when they start receiving payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For members turning 65 from 2023, we have announced previously that we will transfer their Ordinary and Special Account savings into their Retirement Account, up to their cohort Full Retirement Sum, when they are eligible to start payouts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To provide greater flexibility to members, we will make this transfer when they choose to start receiving payouts instead.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will also be the point when we automatically include eligible members in CPF LIFE.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members who are not automatically included can still opt in to join CPF LIFE.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members can still voluntarily transfer Ordinary and Special Account savings into their Retirement Account up to the current Enhanced Retirement Sum at any time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members can continue to withdraw based on the current rules.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Next, we will also make it easier for members to build up their retirement nest egg.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The CPF Board has several schemes which members can tap on to grow their CPF savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also allow CPF members to make cash top-ups or CPF transfers to their Special Account or Retirement Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They can also do so for their loved ones.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To make it easier for members to build up their CPF savings through these schemes, we will refine the relevant tax relief and top-up limit rules.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Currently, members can enjoy tax relief when topping up via these schemes, but the rules in place are different.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To align the rules for both schemes, tax relief for Voluntary Contributions to MediSave Account for employees will be provided to the giver, instead of the recipient.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This cap will be shared between the Retirement Sum Topping-Up scheme and Voluntary Contributions to MediSave Account for employees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To facilitate planning for members, we will also simplify the top-up limit for Voluntary Contributions to MediSave Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, the limit for employees depends on two sets of figures – the Basic Healthcare Sum and the CPF Annual Limit, which is the maximum amount of mandatory and voluntary contributions a member can receive in a calendar year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As members can only know whether they have reached the Annual Limit at the end of each year, this creates some uncertainty for members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, going forward, the top-up limit for employees will be simplified to depend only on the Basic Healthcare Sum.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Basic Healthcare Sum in 2021 is $63,000, while the Annual Limit is $37,740.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you assume that Jane currently has $50,000 in her MediSave Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Assume also that her total mandatory contributions for 2021 will amount to $35,000 and that she makes no voluntary contributions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Based on the new rule, she instantly knows that she can contribute up to $13,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is the $63,000 limit on the Basic Healthcare Sum minus the $50,000 which is currently in her MediSave Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: She can contribute up to $13,000 to her MediSave Account – and this is the headroom between the Basic Healthcare Sum and her current MediSave Account balance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Under the current rules, however, she also needs to be mindful and to consider the Annual Limit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, that means that only at the end of the year will she know that she can contribute up to $2,740 which was the original $37,740 minus $35,000 – because this is the headroom between the Annual Limit and her contributions for the year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we will simplify this for our members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Bill also makes various amendments to streamline the administration of CPF schemes, thereby increasing efficiency for members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are mainly technical changes to refine existing policies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Please allow me to give you three examples.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, the CPF Act will be amended to refine how beneficiaries receive CPF assets, both un-nominated and nominated, upon members’ passing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is in line with ongoing efforts to disburse such assets more quickly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Depending on whether such CPF assets are nominated or not, they are disbursed via different routes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Un-nominated CPF monies are transferred to the Public Trustee’s Office for disbursement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Public Trustee’s Office then has to trace and verify each and every rightful beneficiary to disburse the monies to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Public Trustee’s Office will streamline this process, to enable an eligible beneficiary to receive unnominated CPF monies as a Beneficiary Representative on behalf of all other beneficiaries with their consent, for amounts not exceeding $10,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With this change, the application and verification processes will be simpler for eligible cases.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beneficiaries can expect to receive their monies sooner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The process will still remain unchanged for amounts that exceed $10,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nominated CPF monies are disbursed by CPF Board.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since 2011, the Board has made automatic disbursements to qualifying nominees without requiring them to make an application.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Over the years, CPF Board has continuously relaxed the qualifying criteria to allow more nominees to receive their bequeathed monies without application, which can be particularly helpful for those who need to tap on bequests to defray post-mortem expenses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As of this year, there is no longer any threshold for the amount of nominated monies that can be automatically disbursed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to extend this automatic disbursement to nominees with bequeathed discounted Singtel shares which are purchased under the Special Discounted Shares scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Currently, such nominees are unable to benefit from this convenience as CPF Board has to wait for nominees to instruct whether they wish to have these shares transferred to their own CDP accounts, or liquidated.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the shares remain unclaimed after seven years, CPF Board will liquidate them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the CPF Act amendments, unless otherwise instructed, such shares will be liquidated six weeks after the Board is notified of a member’s death.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: CPF Board will exercise discretion for cases where more time is required to trace beneficiaries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The sale proceeds will then be automatically disbursed, together with other nominated CPF monies, to the nominees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the shortening of the holding duration for discounted Singtel shares that I have just mentioned, this percentage is expected to increase further as more can then benefit from automatic disbursement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This leaves behind a very small group of nominees who have chosen to delay the disbursement of bequests, which could result in the deceased member’s CPF monies remaining in his CPF accounts for up to seven years today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This timeframe should be more than sufficient for beneficiaries to make arrangements to claim nominated monies from CPF Board.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, nominees continue to have the right to claim the nominated monies at any time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will, similarly, adjust the disbursement process for assets in dormant CPF accounts, which form the minority and likely belong to deceased members.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Specifically, once a member’s account is deemed dormant, we will liquidate the member’s discounted Singtel shares and stop retaining the monies, including accrued interest, in the account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to reassure all members that if CPF Board subsequently learns that a dormant member is alive, the Board will restore the monies to the member’s original accounts with interest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Again, let me reiterate that there is no change to CPF beneficiaries’ right to make claims at any time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We recognise that a small percentage of monies remain unclaimed, despite CPF Board’s efforts to reach out to the beneficiaries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nonetheless, CPF Board will continue its efforts to reduce the incidence of unclaimed monies, via a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes regularly reminding nominees to make claims if they have not done so via letters, email, SMS and WhatsApp, educating and reminding members to make nominations, and making the nomination process as easy as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Specifically, the amendment is a technical update to cater for grants automatically issued to eligible members but who, subsequently, choose not to meet continuing eligibility conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is to be fair to the majority of other members who maintain their eligibility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To be clear, this amendment is not about allowing the Government to recover grants provided erroneously to ineligible individuals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The continuing condition here is that members do not reverse the top-ups that had qualified them for the matching grant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House may find that the CPF Act can be quite complicated.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In particular, section 15 on withdrawal from the Fund has 43 subsections.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have simplified this section for better readability while continuing to provide flexibility to cater to members' evolving needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This sums up the key amendments under the CPF (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Retirement and Re-employment (Amendment) Bill supports seniors in working longer should they wish to and choose to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The CPF (Amendment) Bill simplifies the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Together, these Bills will support Singaporeans to earn more and to save more as we continue to enhance our employment and CPF policies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is currently facing two major trends.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans are not only living longer, but also more energetic and spending more years in a healthy stage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are many factors contributing to this, mainly because of our better quality of life and better healthcare amenities, and that people are more aware of the importance of healthy living and live a more fulfilling life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, because of the rise in life expectancy of Singaporeans, we are also facing a second major trend, which is a major shift in our demographics.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have now entered a phase of rapid ageing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These two trends mean that, first, Singaporeans are now healthy enough to work longer and stay active in the workforce if, they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They extend their active working lives, earn more, save more and enhance their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For those who have yet to reach the statutory retirement age, employers cannot stop employing these workers simply because of their age.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, we must also give the employers some flexibility and allow them to adjust the nature of work, role in the company and working conditions for that employee.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are a few issues that we have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, have the employers adjusted their mindset regarding age discrimination and adopted a more positive attitude, and proactively utilised manpower supplement brought about by the increase in the retirement age?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, how to adjust their expectations and manage changes in employment terms which can be based on part-time re-employment or time-based employment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In terms of the employment contract, has the employee and the employer come to a consensus?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Third, in terms of job redesign, there is more work for the Tripartite partners to come work together to redesign jobs that are more suitable for older workers so as to attract more older Singaporeans to join the workforce and help companies raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fourth, with the extension of our work-life, we should also make the necessary policy adjustment when we plan employee training.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, can middle-aged employees be allowed to further their studies in our Institutes of Higher Learning to upgrade their knowledge and skills and improve their re-employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need new thinking on this front and I hope that the Government can reconsider this when formulating policies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must clarify this so that Singaporeans do not misunderstand the intention of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to seek a few clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Does he see uneven readiness among the bigger and smaller companies, among the different industry segments, global versus local companies and employees of different wage profiles?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Does he see different levels of readiness in employers adjusting to the rise in retirement and re-employment age?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I mentioned in my Chinese speech there are some concerns about contractual terms and whether the workers are prepared for those changes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, to what extent can we reduce the dependence on foreign manpower with the raising of the retirement and re-employment age, especially for the PMETs, as there will be a bigger pool of experienced workers for businesses to tap on?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fourthly, following the progressive raising of the retirement age, will there be further measures to counter age discrimination and importantly, to step up monitoring of undesirable employment practices?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fifth, with the employment runway of workers extended, will the Government institute new policy measures to help workers stay employable?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among others, would the Government see the need to introduce, for example, mid-career sabbatical leave so that workers can take a longer break during their mid-careers and to stay charged up for a longer working career?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Or to allow mature students to become students again by allowing them to admit to the Institutes of Higher Learning to pursue new disciplines and to acquire new professional expertise?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Or whether there will be further SkillsFuture support for senior workers?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that the Minister can clarify this so that there will be no misunderstanding on this part.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the individual, it enhances financial security, independence and for some, provides a sense of purpose.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This also benefits society as active seniors are more able to provide for themselves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would enable the state Budget to be allocated to other areas of need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a step in the right direction, which I support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, Sir, if we truly believe in active ageing, it is worth reviewing whether there should be a prescribed minimum retirement age at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, I would note that there are many employees in the private sector who are not subject to a mandatory retirement age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The prescribed retirement age applies more to the public sector and unionised employees.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, continuing to have a minimum retirement age set out in law has a signalling effect on society as to the value workers above that age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, life expectancy in Singapore has increased by approximately three years every 10 years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These ages are merely averages and do not take into account many who live far longer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate how longevity impacts retirement decisions, I would like to share a conversation I had some months ago with a cousin of mine, a retired engineer now in his mid-80s.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He shared that when he and his wife retired 30 years ago, they had no idea that they would live this long.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He lamented that had they known that they still had so many more years to go, they would have worked longer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If an octogenarian can reflect on his life span in this manner today, what about us or younger cohorts who are likely to live longer?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even when the retirement age goes up to 65, the prospect of having insufficient savings to fund another 30 years of living expenses and medical costs is real.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We often hear that foreign manpower is needed to supplement our local workforce.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the COVID-19 pandemic has taught us a very painful lesson about how we have managed our low-wage foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Poor conditions in our crowded foreign worker dormitories have contributed to the spread of the virus.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government mantra has always been that Singapore needs to continue improving productivity instead of relying on increases in labour inputs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In our push towards leveraging on technology, it is likely that more jobs in different sectors will be redesigned to be less reliant on physical strength, making them suitable for senior workers to fill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Third, we must ask whether having a prescribed minimum retirement or re-employment age is sensible for the parties concerned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The fact is that the universe of employees is very diverse.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those with health problems may not be able to work when they reach 60 years old while others can go on for much longer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this, I am not clear how far having a prescribed minimum retirement age protects the worker from being dismissed on account of age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our labour market is one of the freest in the world with hiring and dismissal happening efficiently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Most employment contracts have a termination clause with either employer or employee being able to walk away from the contract by giving just one or two months' notice or payment in lieu of notice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: No reasons need to be given for the termination of service in such situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This change in policy has the potential to give employees protection against ageism in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has argued for anti-discrimination legislation previously and we welcome this announcement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We believe that the proposed law should proscribe discrimination based on age and we look forward to the opportunity to contribute to that debate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To most people, that would not be a life well-lived.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Seniors may well decide to reprioritise their time and devote themselves to their grandchildren or charitable causes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Society could very well be better off if they did so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What I am advocating is that instead of having a decision forced on them at a certain age, we empower our seniors to make their own choice in this matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In closing, it will be appropriate to quote from a Singaporean who has advocated that there be no retirement age, none other than our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2010, on the 30th Anniversary of the Singapore National Employers Federation, Mr Lee spoke at a dialogue with senior managers, Government officials and unionists.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He told them that there should be no retirement age for workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He called on older workers to change their mindsets and to continue working, even if for less pay or for a younger boss.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He said, and I quote, "Many of our workers have a preferred retirement and then they die early.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If you start saying, 'Oh, I am old', and you start reading novels and playing golf or playing chess, well, you are on the way down", unquote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we are truly non-ageist, we should leave retirement and re-employment ages to choices made by individuals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a safety net, we should enact an anti-discrimination law that prohibits employment decisions based on age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Retirement and Re-employment Act came into force in 2012, because of three main factors, namely, a longer life expectancy of the current population, a tightening labour market with a shrinking citizen population and the need for talent management and retention.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, the abovementioned needs continue to exist and underscore the importance of the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Although COVID-19 has challenged the labour market, the Tripartite Partners agree that “the important work to enable older employees to continue working if they are able and willing to do so, must continue.” While I am heartened that the Tripartite Partners remain committed to supporting the re-employment of older workers, I am concerned of more companies not re-employing existing older workers in view of the uneven and uncertain outlook.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I know of some companies who have resorted to making payouts under the Employment Assistance Payment, EAP for short, as an easy and cost-efficient way of circumventing their re-employment obligations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, this situation is in some way exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the life expectancy of individuals increase over the years, together with the mounting pressures on the sandwich generation, it is crucial that we ensure that all older workers who are keen and able to work, can continue to do so, with reasonable adjustments to their re-employment terms.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Accordingly, the EAP should not be used as an easy way out to avoid re-employing older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead, it should only be offered after a thorough review, as a last resort – if the employer cannot find any internal vacancy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To that end, I would like to raise six suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If there is a sizeable increase in the minimum and maximum EAP payable, this might serve to deter companies from cursorily reviewing internal vacancies with a view to letting go of older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Companies may have a greater incentive to find suitable internal vacancies for older workers to work at and be paid for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If push comes to shove and employers genuinely have no other options but to let go of older workers, at least the increased EAP amount would serve to tide them through a longer period of unemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to ensure that the EAP sum provided is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We do not want our older workers to be living from hand to mouth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I, therefore, submit that the Tripartite Partners continue to work at and review the mutually agreed increment in both the minimum and maximum EAP sums, to cater to the increased median wages, changing employment landscape and increased cost of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, additional tiers of unemployment income support for Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs) who are involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The findings of the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce Report show that mature PMEs are particularly precarious when retrenched during the current downturn due to higher costs of living as they provide for both older and younger dependants; longer time periods taken to find a new job in view of their age and lack of relevant skillsets; and increased propensity to suffer from wage loss on re-entry to employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: PMEs shared that an unemployment income support could provide some breathing space for them to retrain, upgrade their skills and look for suitable employment, while helping to alleviate their anxieties and ensure that those who are unaware of avenues of help do not fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I, therefore, suggest that the Government consider an unemployment income support coupled with active labour market policies for all workers, including mature PMEs, who are involuntarily unemployed, and for the Tripartite Partners to study this carefully in greater detail.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, the PME Taskforce Report also found that despite being active in their job search and undergoing training, mature PMEs who were retrenched had difficulties in securing a job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If a new company takes on another company’s re-employment obligations, the short-term salary support from the Government would be particularly useful in easing its re-employment obligations with respect to the mature worker transferred.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Fourth, while the current framework provides flexibility in job negotiations for re-employed employees, we need to safeguard against companies’ exploitations of such flexibilities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Further, with the requirement for written justifications on material changes to the employment terms or sudden lack of internal vacancies, the company bears the burden of justifying that such changes are reasonable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The company cannot simply state that the employee rejected its reasonable re-employment offer as a basis for not paying EAP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Fifth, even as we embrace digital transformation, we urge employers to continue training and upgrading older staff to acquire the necessary skills to minimise the digital and tech inequality.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Where there are incentives and support schemes, to tap on these support schemes and send older workers for training and skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Lastly, through the COVID-19 pandemic, we have seen many changes in the work environment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Just to name a few: businesses have pivoted to online platforms, employees have been working from home and international conferences are held online.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These non-exhaustive lists of examples show us collectively that Singaporeans are agile enough to adapt to various changes and curve balls that the pandemic has thrown at us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As Singapore marches towards the "next normal", I would like to encourage employers to consider how various jobs can be redesigned and re-examined to allow for older workers to continue working.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In so doing, companies may consider the relevant skill sets the employees have and their experiences gleaned over the years, to match any needs that the business may have.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For instance, if a person was employed in a marketing role, a job redesign could involve not just marketing work to external parties, but possibly internal communications, usage of digital platforms and social media and/or pitching of ideas to senior management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Crucially, older workers may also take on the role of mentoring younger employees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead, I urge employers to adopt a change in mindset.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is loosely translated to mean that having an elder at home can be likened to having a treasure at home.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I believe this is also applicable in the work context as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Older employees have amassed a wealth of experience over the years in their specialised areas of work and it would be our loss if we do not tap on this treasure while still available.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is something about decades of work experience, tenacity, soft skills and accumulated knowledge that cannot be quantified, much less deemed as irrelevant for the purposes of re-employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are all laudable objectives, consistent with the overarching mission of the CPF, which is "to enable Singaporeans to have a secure retirement through lifelong income, healthcare financing and home financing." While I am fully supportive of the amendments, I have the following questions from an employment perspective for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Under the CAYE Scheme, Government agencies will deduct and transmit a portion of payment due to SEPs into their respective MediSave accounts, for convenience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, I understand that take-up of the CAYE in the public sector is very encouraging.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In view of that, would the CAYE Scheme be expanded to include the private sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If so, does MOM foresee any resistance from the private sector?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How else may the CAYE Scheme be expanded to help freelancers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If expanded, it would help more freelancers, particularly those who render services to companies in the private sector, keep up with their MediSave contributions and provide greater financial protection against health issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, under the CAYE Scheme for Government projects, the Government essentially deducts a portion of monies due to the SEPs and transmits it to the SEPs' MediSave Accounts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As this House would know, the COVID-19 pandemic has had a decimating effect on the lives and livelihoods of SEPs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With the circuit breaker measures that were implemented last year, together with the existing restrictions on social gatherings, the events and performing arts sector has almost come to a standstill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Their current earnings are a far cry from their earnings prior to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In view of the above, would there be possible circumstances in which SEPs can opt out of the CAYE Scheme, as they may need the monies to tide through this rough patch?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If so, what are some examples of such circumstances?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, in the context of employment relationships, both the employers and employees make CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even as the distinction between SEPs and employees is increasingly blurred, with some countries recognising SEPs as "workers", perhaps service buyers could be required to make CPF contributions for SEPs too?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To be clear, the existing CAYE scheme applicable in the public sector only requires the Government to take a portion of the fees belonging to the SEP, to be credited to the SEP's Medisave account.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As a member of the People's Action Party (PAP) Seniors Group, I am delighted to participate in this debate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope we can increase the retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70, sooner than later, ahead of our target in 2030.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In January 2019, the PAP Senior Group put forth a position paper to empower our seniors to live with purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One of the key recommendations called for a gradual increase in our seniors CPF contribution rate, given that their rate is currently less than that of younger workers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: That same year, the Government agreed to this proposal.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, when the pandemic struck, our Government froze this specific commitment for seniors, so as to help as many companies as possible stay afloat.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While I understand and support this necessary action, I hope the Government can resume the planned increase at the earliest possible time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some sectors are doing well, some are staying afloat and some are frankly struggling.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is something that many of our colleagues from PAP Senior Group would like to see.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the next few months, my fellow colleague from the senior group, Deputy Speaker Jessica Tan, will spearhead an intense effort to engage our senior workers and to solicitate their feedback.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We hope to identify win-win solutions for both senior workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We hope to help seniors to not just improve their employability, but also the equality of their employability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even before the start of our consultation, I have already heard a number of useful suggestions, including disallowing companies from asking the last drawn salaries or the age of applicants.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will share what we have heard from our senior workers in good time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Last, I hope our Government continue to find new ways to help our seniors workers, especially those in their 60s.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I note that NTUC and SNEF have recently submitted some excellent ideas to the Government to help matured Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These ideas will go far to support workers in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, even if we get our upcoming anti-discrimination legislation right, even if we continue to raise our retirement age and re-employment age, our senior workers above 60 will still be very vulnerable to being displaced.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And if they are displaced, it will be very hard for them to find the next full-time job.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, we would need to explore and accelerate new employment models such as micro-jobs and job-sharing for seniors above 60.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And we may need the Government to spearhead this effort, to demonstrate its full potential to the private sector.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I have spoken about micro-jobs on several occasions in Parliament and I think it is time for us to seriously look into that.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And to extend our seniors employability as long as possible, it will be helpful if MOM can convene a panel of medical experts to advise our industries to determine how long our senior professionals and skilled workers can work for in specific industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, the panel can advise companies on how to maximise work opportunities for surgeons, without compromising on patient safety.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The panel can advise companies on how long pilots can continue flying a plane and whether that length depends on the number of passengers sitting on the same plane?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because without an evidence-based decision-making process, the employment outcome in many industries will be driven by supply and demand for workers and a number of industries will adopt an unnecessary conservative approach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means that a number of our senior workers, especially those above 60, could prematurely lose the chance to work, even with the Retirement and Re-employment Act in place.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For many of our seniors, work creates a sense of mission.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is critical to empower our seniors to age with purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Bill discussed today is an important step to strengthen senior employability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: MOM has done a lot, but there is a lot more to do.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And even as we manage to safeguard the health of our vast majority of seniors through this pandemic, a number of seniors today feel a sense of despair, more than in recent years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because our seniors are more impacted by social distancing measures compared to the rest, because our seniors have reduced opportunities to interact with others and to stay relevant, and because our seniors feel a deep sense of isolation amidst the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of both Bills put forth in this debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This move follows the trend evident in many other advanced economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Next year, the United States will raise the age where one is able to draw a full public pension or Social Security benefits, what is typically referred to as the Full Retirement Age, to 67 for those born in 1960.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: France has sought, with limited success, to raise this retirement age of 62, by two years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this year, Japan raised its retirement age to 70, while Australia and Spain will gradually hike the retirement age to 67 in the years ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since Singapore does not have a pay-as-you-go system, the usual justification for countries raising their retirement ages to ensure that their state pension systems are able to remain financially viable in light of an ageing and longer living population, does not apply here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is instead relevant is the legally mandated age where one's employer is able to request that one retires.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, the relevant motivation for us choosing to raise the retirement age is different as it should be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is a recognition that the nature of jobs in the modern economy are often dramatically different from those of yesteryear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most of the menial back-breaking jobs of the past have now, been replaced with machinery and technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accordingly, many jobs are now far less physically demanding, thereby permitting the modern worker to continue performing these jobs at a very high level, regardless of their age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, a number of hard and soft skills, such as technical, oral or interpersonal skills may, like fine wine, even improve with age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, most of the more sophisticated jobs in the modern economy often require an extended period of education and training, especially if they pursue graduate degrees or endure mid-career retraining and reskilling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, of course, coming from an over-educated individual who only completed his formal educational journey the year he turned 30.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While such an extended period of human capital formation is both valuable and positions the worker well for their subsequent career, it also implies that they begin their formal employment journey later than usual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It seems unfair to cut the employment work life's short just by dint of their extended education and training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans are living longer and the number of those entering their 60s and 70s will also swell.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is therefore imperative that we accommodate and extend the work horizon to allow these individuals to continue to participate in meaningful productive activity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If they so wish, such engagement can also positively impact the mental and physical health and delay the onset of memory loss, depressive symptoms and even physical disability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is the official position of the Workers' Party and one reiterated in this House most recently, by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, when he was a Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP) in the 13th Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this is not a call for our workers to continue working themselves into the grave, nor is it a call to postpone the official age of access to CPF savings, a point I will return to later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This call should also be seen as an implicit call to remove discrimination in the workplace on the basis of age, a position that the Workers' Party has likewise championed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With no clear retirement age, employers can no longer use the excuse that hiring a worker with a short runway before they are officially forced to retire, would be an inferior business decision, compared to hiring a younger worker with no such retirement constraint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One natural concern with such a proposal is that doing so could inhibit the renewal of the workforce, as the elderly take up jobs that would otherwise be filled by younger workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding the fact that there are no legal impediments to replacing senior workers with junior ones, regardless of the retirement age, we should not rely on legal crutches to do what managers ought to be doing, which is to make the difficult decision of firing workers if and when necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything, the solution requires a realignment of cultural practices that keep unproductive workers in their positions, rather than keeping an artificial legal retirement age in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the economy where this issue is most chronic, Japan, does have an economy-wide retirement age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, its presence has not alleviated the problem of displacement, which suggests that the solution to excessive youth unemployment lies clearly lies elsewhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The other counter-argument, which is almost the opposite of the first, is that a clear retirement age prevents frivolous firings since employers cannot use the excuse that an employee is, generically speaking, too senior, if they are 57 as opposed to 67.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this argument fails to hold up to theoretical scrutiny.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Why would an employer wait for an underperforming employee to reach any level of seniority before they replace them?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will be far more straightforward to simply grant such workers a severance package and release them, regardless of age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nor does this argument actually work in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have many residents who approached me and shared with me how they were, indeed, let go a number of years before retirement and how they subsequently faced difficulty securing a job because employers deemed them too close to retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, if anything, a fixed retirement age operates to the detriment of workers and does not appear to have inhibited the retrenchment of workers themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am heartened that Minister Tan has made this point clear in his speech earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans should be empowered to make their own informed choices about the manner by which they wish to draw on their hard-earned retirement savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so also permits those nearing retirement to be more creative in the manner by which they balance their employment and retirement choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, a 60-year-old banker may wish to shift gears towards consultancy or adjunct teaching on a part-time basis but, nevertheless, wish to supplement his or her income with a modest CPF payout.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This does not mean, of course, that we do not design incentives to encourage our seniors, especially if they remain in the workforce, to postpone their CPF withdrawals to benefit from the compound interest and, thereby, allow for larger payouts when they eventually make their withdrawals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To my mind, nudges of this form are a far more palatable approach to encouraging individually beneficial retirement choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In other words, it will allow our people to retire after a long struggle with dignity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Similar provisions are made for the re-employment age.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The need to make such legislative provisions arises from the fact that life expectancy has vastly increased and, along with it, people can make choices on how to divide the gains in the number of years between work and retirement.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Evidence from several developed economies shows that an increasing fraction of people in their 60s have chosen to remain active in the labour force since the mid-1990s.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Data from the Singapore Yearbook of Manpower Statistics 2021 show that for those in the age group 60 to 64 years, the male labour force participation rate increased by more than 10 percentage points from 2010 to 2020.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For the age group 65 to 69 years, the male labour force participation rate increased by more than 15 percentage points.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Corresponding figures for the female labour force participation rate for these corresponding age groups showed even bigger percentage point increases, although they remained below the male labour force participation rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For the age group 55 to 59 years, there was also a significant increase in the female labour force participation rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The question: what factors account for the rise in labour force participation rate of older workers in recent decades?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, improved health, by itself, does not explain the rise in labour force participation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This is because data of today's developed economies shows that while the mortality rates at older ages have steadily declined during the past several decades, the labour force participation rate, especially for men, exhibited a U-shaped curve, declining before steadily rising since the mid-1990s.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, changes in the eligibility ages for retirement benefits and rules on disability insurance in the social security system in these countries seem to better explain variations in the labour force participation rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As health has improved, along with the increased life expectancy, people might choose either to work or to engage in meaningful activities that do not necessarily generate an income.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, across education groups, those with more years of education have higher labour force participation among older workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Those with a more rewarding career in the earlier phase of their life cycle are more likely to choose to work when they are older.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As the share of our older population with tertiary education increases, this is likely to lead to higher labour force participation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, various factors, including labour-saving technological improvements in the household sector, such as household appliances, and more years of education have led to a steady rise in labour force participation among women.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The rise in labour force participation rate for women in many of these developed countries occurred earlier, earlier almost by a decade, in many of these developed countries.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: By the early 1980s, there was a relentless, steady increase in labour force participation rate among women.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This rise in labour force participation among women may have the effect of causing higher labour force participation among men if the couples agree to retire at the same time – the so-called "working wife effect".

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, if women bear the additional responsibility of providing care to their much older parents, this may discourage them from working in their late 50s to their mid-60s.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, on the whole, there are factors that clearly had been at work, not just in Singapore but in many developed countries, tending since the 1990s, to raise the labour force participation rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The main point, though, is that people now have an ability to choose how to divide the additional years of their life between retirement and work.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, Singapore's continued growth as a mature economy will be important in order to generate the demand for the skills of our older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I support both Bills and I will speak on the Retirement and Re-employment (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That report was titled "Strengthening Support for Older Workers".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is the subject of the amendments today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I wish to draw that similarity to frame it in such a way that I think will make it easier for all of us, inside and outside of this House, to see what it is that we are trying to do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The first similarity is that both these challenges – ageing population and ageing workforce, locally and climate change – is that they are both very damaging if they are not properly addressed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In the case of climate change, one specific known threat to Singapore would be that of global warming leading to rising sea levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In that scenario, if we do not build up sufficient defences early and well enough, the result will be a loss of coastal areas as the sea level rises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is why the Government, as announced by the Prime Minister and has begun to be put into budgets, will invest heavily to raise the foundation level of critical infrastructure to be well above current sea levels and to build sea walls in order to increase our coastal protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we must do likewise to help our ageing local workforce so that they are not only better protected but would also continue to be a valuable contributor to our economic dynamism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think we all agree it is not right.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But it is there, to a greater or lesser degree.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On this journey that we all want to be on to reduce it, if possible, to eliminate it someday, we continue to have to deal with the reality that while it exists, and it does now, what is it that we must do to accord the necessary protection for our workers?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And it was for this reason, that the Tripartite Workgroup on older workers debated long and hard as the first terms of reference that was set for it, on whether that statutory retirement age for older Singaporean workers is still relevant and needed, at least for the coming decade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I hear several Members speaking about the need for that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I just want to give a little bit of background as to the thinking when we debated this within that workgroup.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The basic question we ask ourselves is supposing there is no ageism in the workplace and therefore, employers are more than happy and will always employ older workers who are willing and able to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Then, it is okay with these companies and it does not matter if we have a statutory retirement age because the company will just continue to employ.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They are not in any way, held back by a statutory retirement age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But in the opposite scenario, where you have companies whose practices are ageist, then it is not so simple in the absence of some strong signal from the tripartite partners, from the Government, in law, I think we can understand that these tendencies will become more pronounced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As it is, we hear examples already cited that residents come to us and say that some of them might have been let go of even as they get into middle age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And they find it more difficult to get a new job and when they do get a new job, the chance of not matching the old terms is quite high.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we ask ourselves, if indeed there is no ageism anywhere around and age equals experience, equals value and is fully appreciated, then why are we having this scenario?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And if you are having this scenario, why is it therefore, not good for us to continue to put in the necessary protections?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, it was along those lines that we discussed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In summary, if there is no ageism, having a statutory retirement age does no harm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If there is, this gives you a strong signal to think again and do not resort to ageist practices so easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, beyond the legality of it, it sends a clear signal to employers on what tripartite partners want businesses and organisations to focus on, namely, to find and put in place effective ways to keep our older workers sharp on the job and not cause them to become a liability prematurely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, I certainly support further efforts to protect older workers against ageist workplace practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And in this regard, I look forward to the outcomes of the Tripartite Workgroup on workplace discrimination that MOM has initiated a few months ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If you look at it that way then, statutory retirement age and re-employment age are like a pair of sea walls, built for our older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They stand as visual reminders of our nation's commitment to protecting our older workers as an asset.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is not merely done to achieve some philosophical ideal, but it is done for a very practical reason.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This safeguards the longer-term resilience while tending to the immediate challenges faced by both companies and their workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I hope that companies and workers alike would draw comfort and confidence from observing this move, knowing that our Government and tripartite partners will always act in the overall best interest of both our workers and companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, in other words, the Government is co-paying with the employers for the improvement for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This would certainly make it easier for the employer's to also implement this and to benefit the workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, I hope to seek this clarification from Minister whether that package would be put up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Building sea walls are necessary but they are not sufficient to ensure key infrastructure can keep above the waves of change, which is why it is necessary to raise the foundation level well above sea level, so that these places can stay dry longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And in this light too, I say, it is similar to what we must continually do in order to shore up the employment and employability of our older workers for the journey ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Over the years, the Government has introduced numerous hiring and training incentives that favour the older worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Examples would include the Senior Employment Credit, the Senior Worker Early Adopter Grant, the Part-time Re-employment Grant and various others as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These financial incentives have indeed been very helpful in lowering the cost of hiring of older workers and therefore increase the numbers hired.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I am glad that the efforts of the tripartite partners and the responsible actions by the vast majority of firms have kept the employment rate of older workers stable despite COVID-19's onslaught.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Government has also provided preferential subsidies for the training of older workers for many years now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While wage subsidies serve to lower the cost of hiring of older workers and they would certainly help, they are actually also not the longer-term safeguard that is needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They are necessary, helpful but they are not the longer-term safeguard that is needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For analogy again, you can imagine that they are very, very good sandbags and flood barriers that you can mount right at local level and that helps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But what they do not do is that they do not reduce the inherent vulnerability of that premises to flooding, if the premises itself is too low.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, we must still continue to undertake the hard work of raising the foundation levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is the ultimate way to keep the premises above the rising tides, and in like manner, effective improvement in the employability of older workers is the ultimate way to help as many of our older workers as possible stay above the rising tides of skills obsolescence and workplace value depreciation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There are very clear signs that we need to pay close attention to this area and to act on it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I said earlier that the employment rate of older workers has held steady and even improved slightly between 2019 and 2020, despite COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I would qualify it that this was so for workers aged 55 and above.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC and SNEF co-led a task force – we call it the PME's Taskforce – to examine the needs, hopes and anxieties of PMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To be sure, this anxiety was already there before COVID-19 and it came about partly as a result of business model changes, partly as a result of delayering of middle management and also technological changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must not wait until these folks are near retirement age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This must go hand in hand with ensuring a level playing field for Singaporeans in being considered for job openings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is so that middle aged local workers would not be too easily or prematurely rendered unemployable and have to exit the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Otherwise, legislative improvements, such as the ones that we are considering today, to increase the retirement and re-employment ages would be rendered moot, because they would not even be there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we must help them carry on and then with this extension, they will also benefit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Equally importantly, we must know that policy and incentives themselves are necessary again, but not sufficient to ensure the required outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Effective last mile implementation is critical to ensuring real and sustained outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
