text: First, let us invest even more to further boost the capacity and effectiveness of job retraining and employment facilitation mechanism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must give due credit to the work of WSG, NTUC e2i, SSG and NTUC's Company Training Committees (CTCs) and the Job Security Council (JSC) for each year helping thousands of jobseekers retrain and find new jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And many amongst them would be older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we got to do a study on this and investment what is necessary to expand ahead of that curve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For if we do not get this right, then we will have to face up to a growing pool of displaced, disillusioned and disgruntled older workers in society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Second, let us factor in more episodes of displacement and to configure the help for that in-between.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every worker now must expect multiple episodes of employment through his working life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This means that it will not be lifelong employment for most.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This in turn means that workers will need more help in between jobs to tide over as they job-search, and as they retrain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is especially so in the cases where the job lost was not voluntary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While it remains true that we must not encourage pickiness when it comes to jobseeking, but we must also recognise the real downsides of being forced by circumstances to repeatedly take jobs that pay worse or under-utilise ability, without reasonable alternatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Thirdly, let us review the structuring and conduct of CET or Continuous Education and Training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is common to hear training being divided into two phases – PET or Pre-employment Training, generally the "schooling years", as most people understand it, as well as CET, which is the working years, as many people would understand it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think it would be quite obvious to all of us that investments in Pre-employment Training (PET), over the decades have been immense.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This correctly reflects the Government's recognition of our people as our most important asset, who must be developed and who must be tapped to their fullest potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Government funding for CET, that is the employment part of it – during the working years – has also grown very substantially over the years, via course fee subsidies, absentee payroll, paid internships and conversion programmes for mid-career workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There are also the SkillsFuture credits granted to all Singaporeans aged 25 and above for self-initiated skills development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, a lot of money is also being invested in those areas, especially in more recent years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The fast-changing environment creates a serious uncertainties that confound both workers and companies over what training would be purposeful and for whom.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This generates inertia at the level of the company and the individual.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In other words, I hold back training because I am not very sure what am I supposed to be trained at?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And after I get the training, am I headed for something meaningful?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Or sometimes, it might actually result in, instead of inaction, it goes into aimless training; train for the sake of chalking training hours, for example, which is not the point, because it does not help keep your skills sharp.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And when that happens, you still face a progressive loss of employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The risk is therefore that more and more of our nation's human potential can be wasted this way if the uncertainty continues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To tackle that problem, we cannot tackle it just by introducing more schemes or more subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This must be carefully and seriously studied, so that the current ecosystem can be reshaped to help mid-career mature workers hone and update their skills and strengthen their value and their employability as well as their adaptability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must continue to do so, especially given our ageing local workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must fight ageist workplace practices and give our older workers a chance and a choice to continue working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is so that mature workers and their companies will update their skills more rapidly and purposefully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will then help mature workers grow with their companies and be more able to quickly move into new jobs and into new sectors if they are displaced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This will be crucial in helping mature workers keep their value and sense of security, and view the future with optimism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is to protect him or her from an ageist employer who cites no other reason than age, to say bye bye to him or her.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As the CPF is one of the key financial resources for most Singaporeans, it is imperative that any changes to be introduced are properly communicated and due care be given to enable the public to understand what these changes mean to them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Given there are a number of amendments to be made and a few areas where the specifics to the conditions laid out are not entirely clear, I wish to seek several clarifications.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Does it refer to a health condition, and if so what kind, or does it refer to a financial situation of the said member?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I hope that these discretionary disbursements based on the member’s situation is meant to help supplement their situation and does not have the unintended consequence of putting them in a worse position, should they be relieved of any social assistance programmes or the support scheme being significantly reduced after the lump sum disbursement is made.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Under section 13, lifting the cap annual limit for certain types of voluntary contributions to the Medisave account.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe this move is a welcome one, especially for those self-employed, better enabling and ensuring that their healthcare needs are taken care of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Does the Ministry have any projections on the implications of these changes in the form of retirement adequacy and to what extent will it help the self-employed or those working in the gig economy?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These voluntary contributions can be paid either by the member or from their family members’ contribution.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population in Singapore, whilst the younger generation helps to contribute to their parents' or grandparents’ MediSave accounts and will bridge the immediate support for their healthcare needs, have we considered what are the correlated effect that would be on the family members assisting to top up the CPF of their loved ones?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Will the same issue of healthcare MediSave sufficiency be an issue for the next generation if they do not have sufficient cash set aside for medical purposes or are without additional medical insurance?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think it will be more beneficial for the younger cohort of the working population to be offered financial literacy on how to better manage their retirement needs and in the process learn to balance their own needs versus providing for their parents or the elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Another area is providing a new and simplified process for the distribution of unnominated CPF monies on a member’s death.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Tying this point to the earlier note I made about the discretionary automatic disbursements to the member, if he or she is a beneficiary or nominee of the CPF account from another person, would there be a specified limit that prevents them from receiving any future social support?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And, Sir, going beyond the amendments of the Bill, I would like to raise two other points for further consideration.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Caring for the special needs community and having them included in the scheme is something that I feel passionately about.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I had previously raised in this House regarding the creation of micro jobs to ensure that these individuals when they become young adults, are able to gain some independence and be a part of the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, against the backdrop of changes to the CPF in allowing more relaxation on the withdrawal of CPF monies, I would like to suggest that we also consider how best to safeguard this community and by extension to their families and caregivers in times of need.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For example, the simplification of processes for them to access the funds when their caregivers are no longer around or to apportion more funds for their medical needs as they are more likely to require that on the long run.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Next, rethinking the CPF’s current allocation rates design.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the landscape of work changing and more choosing to embark on flexi work or self-employment, perhaps it is timely in the near future for us to review the CPF’s allocation rates to the three different buckets – the Ordinary Account (OA), the Special Account (SA) and the MediSave Account – to better provide for retirement adequacy whilst ensuring we meet our housing, education and healthcare needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With the current design categorised according to age groups, perhaps it might be worth rethinking if more nuances are required in the current allocation principle and rates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Maximising contribution to the OA during the active income years before increasing the allocation to the SA from 35 to 55 years of age and subsequently for the MediSave to be raised through the SA and OA after a specific age and in line with medical costs during that time period.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is especially so as the nature of work is fast evolving, more are seeking self-employment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The definition of job security and stability do not have the same representation as before.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are also individuals who could be taking on more than two jobs at different stages of their life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Hence, I suggest that a review be undertaken and more holistically ensure that we are able as a nation to better cater for retirement adequacy for all.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We currently have the world’s third highest life expectancy, with the average Singaporean expected to live till about 83 years old.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With better healthcare, this is projected to increase to over 85 in 2040.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As our lifespan increases, it becomes vital that we pay attention to the longevity of our careers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Long gone are the days when it was the norm to join a company and work in the same company for the entirety of one’s career.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There is a new saying, “Career mobility is the new career stability”, and I know that many of our younger workers, particularly the PMETs, live by this axiom.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But how mobile are the careers of our mature workers?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Statistics and ground feedback suggest that it is much harder for mid-career and mature workers to find a new job after being displaced.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: On the ground, we hear of the deep anxieties that mature workers have if they are displaced, particularly if they are close to the retirement age.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is therefore important that we place emphasis on our late-stage career mobility when we are young.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we prepare Singaporeans for a longer career, I hope that the Government’s public education campaigns about retirement adequacy can go beyond financial terms, but also on how to secure fruitful and meaningful work when they reach their silver years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Minister for Manpower himself touched on them during the Parliamentary Sitting last month, where he gave a breakdown of the schemes under the Senior Worker Support Package.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While these schemes have helped Singapore to maintain relatively high levels of senior worker employment rates, the underlying assumption behind these schemes reflects the societal stereotype – that we need to subsidise employers to hire mature workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we extend our retirement and re-employment ages, combined with a rapidly ageing workforce, this will not be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should therefore strive to think of new solutions to encourage companies to view senior workers as assets and not liabilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Perhaps we could provide corporate tax incentives to companies that significantly invest in senior workers, for example, those that actively hire and train over 30% of its workforce above the age of 55.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Perhaps we could provide co-funding for companies that wish to revamp their workspaces to be more inclusive, especially to the needs of senior workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Having schemes that go beyond wage subsidies would encourage companies to pay serious attention to investing in their silver workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to the Mercer CFA Institute Global Pension Index, Singapore has the best retirement system in Asia and ranks 10th in the world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While CPF LIFE can help to close the gap in retirement adequacy, the scheme is meant to cover a basic level of costs during retirement and may not be sufficient for those who do not properly plan for their retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A study published by AIA Singapore in July 2021 reported that 60% of Singaporeans face an uncertain future by not prioritising their retirement planning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a worrying trend and we certainly need to focus on improving the financial literacy of Singaporeans, so that they understand the importance of building a nest egg for their silver years while they are still young.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To help families better plan for their retirement years, the NTUC launched a social enterprise, MoneyOwl, to provide reliable and competent financial advice.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: MoneyOwl’s financial advisers do not operate on commissions, which means that they do not have an incentive to sell consumers products that they do not need.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must strive to help Singaporeans work longer more meaningfully, if they wish to, by changing the narrative of hiring senior workers into a worthwhile investment instead of a hire that comes with hefty Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, keeping seniors in the workforce for as long as they are willing and able, will help ease the manpower situation somewhat.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Legislation will help to ensure consistent fair treatment of senior workers by all employers and deter possible senior worker abuse.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Equally, if not more important than legislation, are the structural changes needed at the workplace, the support needed to help mature workers to better prepare for retirement in addition to the all-important CPF adequacy and MediShield Life, and above all, the need for mindset change on everyone’s part.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst there is general support by both retired and retiring seniors as well as by companies, some of the key questions linger in their minds include: seniors thinking, "Will there be a change in CPF withdrawal age resulting from this amendment?" Well, everyone should be quite glad to hear the Minister confirm that there will be no change to the CPF withdrawal date, which incidentally is a sacred cow, a sacred milestone, not to be touched.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Another question is that if they are re-employed to do the same job, will they get the same compensation?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can seniors, even the so-called retired ones, continue to contribute their experience and skills in building and strengthening Singapore?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As for employers, some of the questions they have on their minds may include: how will this impact the cost of doing business?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Will senior workers be able to pick up the skills and competencies needed for today’s competitive market?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Will they be able to cope with digital disruptions?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How do I implement succession planning without being misconstrued as having an ageism attitude?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And with millennials in search for meaningful roles, should seniors not be making way for them?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All these are very good questions, and many Members in this House have already touched on quite a few of them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For me, I am part of the retiring/retired cohort.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I consider myself very blessed to be reasonably prepared for my second half.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When I was in my 40s, I was recommended the book "Half Time" by Bob Buford and that got me thinking.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Before I turned 50, I attended Cenacle Sister Linda Lizada's retreat on mid-life transition and that started me planning and praying.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have been preparing myself for a meaning and purposeful life beyond the IBM employee pass, which I carried for 33 years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Admittedly, however, it was still a moment of truth to be reckoned with when the day actually came.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, for the many who were less prepared than I, and for some who were even caught by surprise, I empathise with them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I would dare say that most in my generation are generally ill-prepared and cannot quite cope with the drastic physical and physiological change at the point of retirement.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We are the Baby Boomer generation, with strong work ethics and most have given their all to their jobs and growing Singapore's economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, transitioning from active employment to retirement, for many, is like dropping off a cliff.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is a need, therefore, for companies and the communities supported by the Government and civil society to better prepare our senior workers for what I will call the "shoulder season".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With a longer expected lifespan, even the seniors who do not choose re-employment after having worked for almost 40 years, I advocate that, collectively, we start a new focus on the shoulder season.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Ringfence this age demographic, define the benefits, including, perhaps, CPF, especially for this life stage, and build a whole new economy with ancillary services and so on around this social tribe.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Make it a stage of life that people look forward to.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In a brainstorming session with Singapore Human Resources Institute (SHRI), we came up with some ideas for the Public Service and private sector employers to consider.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, organisations will need to be flexible and redesign jobs for part-time work, for shared roles and even cater for permanent work-from-home jobs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Such gig jobs may already be contracted out today but, if they are offered to employees, will help the employees in this age group to apply the skills that they may have decided to pick up and prepare for their shoulder season.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This will also benefit the company as they will be building up their contractual fringe, as termed by Charles Handy in "The Age of Unreason", with trusted employees who may, over time, transition to become external associates paid not by wages but by fees for results produced.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, more companies could join the career trial for mature workers, which gives both parties a trial period before contracting.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations could also facilitate seniors to transition from their functional roles to be advisors, coaches, trainers so as to pass on their wisdom and experience to the next generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Government and the industry could also consider investing in a platform to identify and help match the available supply of senior resources to demand, both paid and voluntary.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Another idea includes, besides restructuring jobs, there is also a need to rethink job positioning, separate seniority, job skill levels and the management span so that it will allow senior civil servants and senior functional heads to continue to contribute in areas where their skill level and experience can be utilised without them feeling that they have been demoted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Along with these structural changes, the need to step up retraining cannot be over-emphasised.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SBF Foundation's Employability Fund supports such initiatives and I thought to share this story of one of the companies in this programme.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The mentee, a trans-shipment manager in his late 60s and who has been with the company for three years, is learning how to use technology – the system and the platform of the company – to do his job.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Despite his age, he is willing to try and learn.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The mentor, a much younger but senior executive who has been with the company for two and a half years, has been helping the mentee to do this virtually due to COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: She scheduled time from her very busy schedule to help the mentee and he has definitely benefited from it.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This intergenerational type of engagement is also good for the soul.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the senior workers, we do need to help ourselves by recognising that performance and attitude are still the best ticket to a mutually satisfying re-employment contract.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The senior worker does have to acknowledge their own energy level, their strengths, their ability to contribute, their attitude and mindset, and recognise that compensation should be tied to the job role and not to their seniority.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The executive director of the Singapore National Employment Federation (SNEF) shared with me that Singaporean companies, generally, support the proposed legislation and are open to hiring senior workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the idea of shared HR services which can serve to enable and support our SMEs to better support the implementation of the legislation and the structural changes needed to achieve the desired outcomes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Preparing our workers for their shoulder season begins with preparing them through their careers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One, promotion should not be by seniority but, rather, by the individuals' performance and capabilities as demonstrated by their work portfolio, including perhaps a willingness to have short working stints in ASEAN markets and elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A second change could be on succession planning.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Succession planning is critical for the sustainability of every organisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, there should be fair practice policies to embrace diversity and inclusion and not be the excuse for discriminating against older employees to make way for younger staff.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To quote Martin Luther King, "No work is insignificant.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All labour that uplifts humanity has dignity." I support both Bills.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For the lucky ones amongst us, it brings with it notions of freedom and leisure, golden years where one is no longer a wage slave.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On the other end of the spectrum, it brings with it negative connotations of decline, withdrawal and fears about whether the money in the bank account would be enough to stretch to the end of the month.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is to address this financing of our retirement that prompted the formation of the CPF system in the first place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our CPF system was introduced in 1955, before the time when some of our present retirees today were born.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Its official mission is to be the bedrock of our social security system, with a strong emphasis on self-reliance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is something that we cannot disagree with and, indeed, most of the residents we do meet tell us that they would love to be in a position to help themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, over the years, the changing structure of our economy, demographics and, indeed, the world we live in has meant that many Singaporeans find themselves in a difficult position today, where no matter how hard or fast they run on the treadmill of life, they find themselves unable to keep up and end up falling off and find it next to impossible to get back on again – and not for want of trying.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our CPF system, as the expressed bedrock of our social security system, has to be sensitive and cognisant of these difficulties experienced by our fellow residents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our CPF policies have, as a response to our changing economy and society, evolved and expanded in an attempt to cover functions beyond merely a savings for retirement, to be used to pay for many of lives' expenses – from the funding of the purchase of our homes to paying for medical expenses for ourselves and our family members.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, at the core of it is the notion that our CPF funds must be kept locked up with a special key and that they would only be unlocked at a certain time and in a certain manner.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may be laudable but it is little wonder that many of our residents do approach us for assistance with CPF matters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am sure that most of us here in this House have come across cases where a loved one, often the sole breadwinner of the family, either passes away unexpectedly or suffers from a condition that results in them being unable to carry on earning an income.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When such unexpected events happen, family members, more often than not, struggle to process the shock and have to make changes to their daily lives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, they often find themselves having to deal with the additional stress and paperwork to unlock CPF funds to tide them through difficult times, which not all are well-equipped to tackle even when not dealing with the grief or shock that colours everything in the overwhelming aftermath of such an unfortunate event.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I would like to request the Minister to clarify what the specified limit would be and how the amount is, ultimately, to be determined.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This does help to prepare us in an ageing society and gives more flexibility to those who are able to do so to better plan for retirement and care needs while still active in the workforce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, could we please have further clarity on whether CPF Board has an estimation of how many people would be affected by this?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to some of the other proposed amendments, I have further comments and would like to seek some more clarifications.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, we welcome the flexibility introduced in clause 5, allowing a member to withdraw funds from his Retirement Account, subject to the condition that they must be receiving an approved annuity stream that is outside of the CPF.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I would like to ask for greater clarity on how such other annuity streams are assessed and, ultimately, approved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Likewise, the same clause introduces automatic withdrawals if the Board is satisfied that the member is suffering from a significant condition, without the need for the member to apply for such withdrawals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The explanatory note further clarifies that this only relates withdrawals from the Ordinary and Special Accounts and not the Retirement Account.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If this is on the understanding that the member is extremely ill or incapacitated, it would mean that it would ease the financial and administrative burden on family members who might need to, otherwise, apply through the Courts or otherwise find additional funds to pay for medical bills or living expenses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Minister also please clarify if automatic disbursements would take place in all cases when a member has a significant condition?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may not be necessarily desirable in cases where the financial circumstances of a member could mean that immediate disbursement of funds is unnecessary.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such an automatic disbursement then may deprive the member of interest on these released funds which would be challenging to obtain in other savings accounts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The current position is that any nominations for recipients of CPF funds upon a member's death is automatically cancelled upon a member's marriage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2010, 9% of the Singapore’s population was aged 65 years and above.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Singapore was then considered as an ageing society.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Singapore has transited from an ageing society in 2010 to become an aged society in 2020, just within a span of 10 years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: That is, we will become a super-aged society like Japan.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many economists consider this as a silver tsunami.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But how do we turn the silver tsunami into a silver lining?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Well, we need more of a whole-of-Government approach to tackle the issue of a super-aged society.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I would like to make some suggestions over three broad areas.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: First, to allow more senior Singaporeans to work as long as possible, where health permits and Singaporeans willing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Second, have flexible housing arrangements to allow as many elderly people as possible to age at home.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Three, to create a National Volunteer Registry to encourage as many seniors as possible to volunteer when they can.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I would suggest to name this programme as the Orange Compass and I would elaborate on the programme later.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many of us would agree that with better nutrition, better medical advancements and better living conditions in Singapore, Singaporeans live longer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Today’s 65 years old is like 55 years old decades ago.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, I totally agree with the amendment in the Retirement and Re-Employment Act to increase the retirement and re-employment age progressively from next year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, almost 60% of the Singapore’s workforce is in PMET jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When they turn 55 years old, their productivity is less likely to decline as compared to the blue-collar workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Even for the blue-collar workers, many are still fit and healthy at 55 years old, their productivity is unlikely to deteriorate significantly when they turn 55 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If that is a reality, the employer’s CPF contribution rate for those below 60 years old would remain at 17% before reducing to 14% for those between 60 and 64 years old, and 10% for those between 65 and 69 years old, and 8% for those who above 70 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To mitigate the financial impact on the employers, we certainly hope that MOM will strengthen the senior worker support package to ease the transition.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Next, I support the NTUC’s efforts to urge the employers to redesign work scope, use automation to reduce manual works so that more seniors can continue to work till 70 years old or beyond.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I continue, I would like to declare my interest as the CEO of ComfortDelGro Taxi.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The retirement age of taxi drivers was last changed and revised in 2012.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With more intelligent safety features like autonomous emergency brake and lane departure alert becoming a norm for taxi, it will be safer for older taxi drivers to drive, provided they pass the stringent annual medical screening.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, the time is ripe to review the retirement age of taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: During my weekly house visits in the past decade, I find that more and more elderly people are staying alone.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With the successful launch of Community Care Apartments in Bukit Batok, I hope HDB can accelerate the launch of Community Care Apartments in more HDB estates, especially the older towns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To encourage more seniors to take up Senior Housing Bonus scheme, I would like to urge HDB to waive the resale levy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will also encourage the seniors to monetise their flat for better retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While waiting for HDB to build more Community Care Apartments, I would like to suggest that MOH and MSF further fund the Senior Activity Centres or SACs at the HDB studio apartments to provide similar services that are planned for the Community Care Apartments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, the SACs can provide care and support services as well as simple home fix services to the existing HDB studio apartments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As we become a super-aged society, it is not tenable to employ more and more foreign workers to take care of the less mobile seniors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The average life expectancy of Singaporean is 84 years old but many are expected to be in poor health in the last 10 years of their life .

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Henceforth, it is important to encourage seniors, near retirement age or for those who just retired to remain active and volunteer to help other seniors who are less mobile or in a poorer health situation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In view of the above, I would like to recommend the Government to start a National Volunteer Registry which I would name "Orange Compass".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Orange Compass could have the following benefits.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It could encourage more abled seniors to volunteer to earn points and the points earned would be able to be kept in the central registry, preferably using block chain technology.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If we can find sufficient sponsors, the points accumulated can be converted to food vouchers, taxi vouchers and so on to mitigate the cost of living for the seniors that volunteer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The points earned can also be kept for the future to exchange for services when the seniors become less abled.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, seniors can volunteer when they are in their 60s and 70s, that is, when they are more abled.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When the seniors are in their 80s, they can use the points accumulated in the registry to exchange for services provided by future volunteers to bring them to the hospital for medical check-ups, for example.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Orange Compass can provide the direction for more abled seniors to volunteer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When the seniors are assured that their volunteer efforts will be recognised, more will volunteer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When the seniors know that their volunteer efforts can be stored securely in the registry and redeem for services in the future, they are more likely to volunteer as well.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, according to the UN definition, a senior is someone who is above 65 years old.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In other words, our population is ageing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Economists often describe an ageing society as a silver tsunami or a silver crisis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I believe that with good planning and Singaporeans working together, we will have the opportunity to turn a silver tsunami into a silver lining and we can truly "see an elder at home as a treasure".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Raising the retirement and re-employment age is the first step, so I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The more important thing is how Singaporeans treat older workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Prof Tommy Koh has called on Singaporeans not to discriminate against older workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, NTUC and SNEF have been working together to accelerate mechanisation and automation, so that blue-collar workers will still be able to do their jobs beyond the age of 65.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In recent years, autonomous driving technology progressed by leaps and bounds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This way, more older Singaporeans can continue to work beyond the retirement age.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, Singaporeans are better educated over the years and more are using their brain power rather than their physical strength, to contribute to the economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, Singaporeans are living longer with medical advancement and accessibility to medical care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, we need to create an environment for Singaporeans to work as long as possible and as long as they are willing, to meet the requirements of the growing economy, rather than tapping more on the foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Increasing the retirement and re-employment age progressively is definitely the right step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Concurrently, we also need to tap on the silver generation for volunteerism as they prepare for retirement.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If coordinated well, the Orange Compass can also help to mobilise the untapped resources to turn the silver tsunami into a silver lining.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Although we have an ageing population, our talent resource in Singapore remains strong.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With a more senior and active workforce, we have a strong foundation of capabilities, experience and knowledge for the next generation of workforce to build upon.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A strong baseline of core capabilities coupled with decades of experience can enable our senior workforce to become more agile and acquire new skills quickly.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But to do this, we need to better map and acknowledge skillsets so that relevant skills can be transferred and applied in a different and dynamic context.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must continue to have an open mind to understand the relevance of past experiences and the transference of related skills in different operating context.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To view individuals for their strengths and how their strengths can be relevant and accretive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the same time, the workforce must continue to adopt a lifelong learning attitude, more so with the objective of being relevant for life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, we must also be pragmatic in our implementation, there are realities with getting on with age.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But given the speed and depth of digitalisation, the working environment can be highly inclusive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is a step in the right direction, but there is much work left to be done.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must make sure that we work hard to unlock this potential.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It gives older workers the opportunity to increase their retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Older workers bring invaluable experience to any organisation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We all know colleagues, friends and family members who can, want and do contribute, long past the current retirement age.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But it is also true that as a person gets older, sometimes, you lose a little in terms of physical ability but also, mentally, you start to lose a bit of sharpness, speed, drive and other priorities become more important.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, let us face it, for a number of our older Singaporeans, they just do not want to have to keep working at the same pace or keep having to reinvent themselves, because work can be a grind, especially if you are in an industry that is being disrupted, especially when there are younger co-workers who are eager to move ahead, who are all too happy to, as we say, "chiong".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And on their part, companies need to be able to create space for these workers to move up the ranks faster.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The re-employment framework has always been given flexibility to employers to adjust re-employment terms and roles.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As the pace of change and disruption in industry only continues to grow faster, more effort will be needed, as called out by the Tripartite Workgroup, to promote more inclusive and progressive workplaces, including redesigning jobs and reskilling, providing more part-time re-employment opportunities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some companies are also looking into how to fractionalise jobs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When doing these, I urge organisations to engage retiring workers on how best to do this; they are often in the best position to propose the most optimal ways.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, retiring workers can and should also plan and propose it themselves, rather than wait for their employers to do it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But whether it is redesigned jobs, part-time or fractionalised jobs, more and more older workers may not stay in the same roles when they enter into re-employment contracts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe, by and large, older workers will accept that there may be commensurate adjustments to their employment terms – wages or benefits.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In a previous response to Parliamentary Questions, then-Minister for Manpower Mrs Josephine Teo shared that the vast majority of re-employed workers in the same job did not experience any cuts to wages and benefits.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is comforting, suggesting that the majority of employers are playing ball, in line with the spirit of re-employment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: However, many of us would have also received appeals from residents, that this is not always the case, such as for my resident Mdm L.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But it cannot be at the expense of long-serving employees.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As the number of older workers on re-employment contracts increases, as a number of re-employment workers who do not stay in the same jobs but are reassigned to different jobs, redesigned jobs, or other adjustments to their roles, or move to part-time status, more attention and protection should be focused on the fair and dignified treatment of re-employed employees, during moments of truth such as retrenchment exercises, which will remain a feature of the landscape, as technology and other disruptions continue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I hope this will be given attention in the implementation of any legislation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, we should continue to review the social safety nets afforded to older workers, lower-income ones especially, so that today’s retirees and future generations get the dignified retirement that they have earned.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The disbursement process today can take a long time and feel quite complex to family members.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is especially the case when there are large families with a claim to the CPF monies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Recently, I had a Meet-the-People Session (MPS) appeal where the case had been in limbo for more than a year, with several back and forth queries with the Public Trustee Office.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The increased efficiency, however, should not come at the expense of the next-of-kin deserving of a share of the funds, particularly in situations where there are family disputes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What recourse does a next-of-kin have in the event that they do not agree with the appointment of the beneficiary representative, or with how the beneficiary representative disburses the CPF monies?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Does it automatically become a private matter to be settled among the beneficiaries, which may or may not result in a Court process or do they continue to have recourse to a public agency which may be more trusted to administer the disbursement process in accordance with the relevant Acts.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the above questions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The CPF Fund is central to Singaporeans of all ages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From prospective home buyers to retirees, the CPF is the joint result of the blood and sweat of Singaporeans and their firm trust in our Civil Service.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, it is a crucial safety net that Singaporeans rely upon to support themselves and their loved ones when the unfortunate strikes – the loss of livelihoods, be it due to economic circumstances, age, infirmity or permanent disabilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It takes conscientious effort to maintain and keep track of one's own bank account and this is especially the case for our senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our pursuit of the bigger, better and faster, Singapore has rapidly morphed itself into a Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The flipside of which is that we risk detaching some of our citizenry as we shed the cocoon of a developing nation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is an uphill battle for many working adults to help their parents navigate finances, and the myriad of accounts at their disposal only complicates the matter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The auto top-up mechanism streamlines the decision-making process of many retirees, some of which could really benefit from this help.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe this to be an important first step towards a more user-friendly and accessible CPF.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, the simplifying of the language of the Act.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Streamlining the headers and process to align the practices with MediSave, for instance, makes the CPF Act more approachable and thereby more effective.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Previously, I have raised the issues of the disconnected – both in terms of digital skills and language for the residents in my constituency – and this step signposts an important direction to make the word of the Law the word of our people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this simplification, however, it is important that we do not lose nuances that protect the same people we have set out to look out for with these changes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As more complicated terms are stripped down, merged or simplified, we need to be clear the intention behind certain changes, as they are not simply a matter of semantics, but whole matters of inclusion and exclusion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is explained in the Bill that this criterion would be "similar" to that of the previous language of "mental and physical incapacity".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I welcome the new lexicon, foremost because it differentiates a disability from one’s identity better than the previous set of language, but I can imagine this new definition, to which the Minister interprets, might prove to be rather ambiguous until tested by real life cases.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rather, there are two issues from this change I am concerned about.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First, if any existing beneficiaries would be left out because of the change in wording.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, this shift in language can send the wrong message to those who are excluded from withdrawing from their CPF because they cannot meet the criteria.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Previously, not being able to withdraw funds, as outlined in section 15AA, would simply mean that they cannot prove that their disabilities incapacitated them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This does not discredit or make light of the condition that they do have; we simply mean that this condition, as bad as it is, does not disempower our residents completely.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is a positive message for those who are rejected, one that affirms that they still have some means to fend for themselves.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In such matters, sensitivity, reason and flexibility must be applied in the first few cases under this amendment and the process may be messy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is my responsibility to raise a word of caution on this matter and it is with time that I trust this interpretation will bring about clarity and trust.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   I wonder if you have discussed with your parents on the issue of savings.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For many senior residents, the best bank for them is called "under the bed" and the most reliable retirement fund is called "secret stash".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that we all have conflicted feelings towards modern finance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, for uncles and aunties who are not familiar with ATMs, many are not resentful or fearful towards CPF.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is not because it is easier to navigate the CPF system or because it is more reliable than the banks.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the contrary, for many people, the complexity of CPF can be daunting and this is something that we should improve on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, for them, the difference is that CPF is trustworthy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They trust in the character, integrity and commitment of the Government.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is contained in CPF is not just money, but also the blood and sweat and trust of the people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This amendment Bill provides provisions for automatic top-ups so that it is more user-friendly for the uncles and aunties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must quicken our steps and allow CPF to become the pillar of a dignified and less stressful retirement life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In all, this amendment is in line with what I stand for.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It brings law to the ground where it matters, it makes the law easier to understand, it makes the content of the law more useful to the people it is to serve.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With time, I trust that the initial ground messiness will be resolved with sensitivity, caution and flexibility of ground issues.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now, onto the Retirement and Re-employment Act (RRA).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a country like ours with no natural resources and hinterland, our source of pride and success has always been our people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The emerging generation of seniors is perhaps the most well-educated, healthy and capable of their age group in history.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are a diverse, dynamic group with varying interests and passions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, medical and technological advancements of today provide the prospects of a full and enriched life even as our seniors continue to age.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As people live longer, lives must be viewed through a different set of lenses.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, we are now looking at a 100-year life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead of the conventional way of thinking about life in three phases: education up to the early 20s, working life until the 60s and then a long retirement.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must now be prepared for a multi-stage life, perhaps a more flexible life structure where the end goal is no longer retirement and stopping of work, but one where time as a resource is redistributed differently.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, approaching our silver years in life need not be merely confined to the idea of retirement and fading off into career obscurity, but rather be seen as an opportunity to live meaningful and happier mature years as we continue to contribute to society while staying active and healthy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At this juncture, I would like to share an inspiring story of my constituent, Mdm Lucy Ho, who is 71 years young.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lucy worked in SIA Engineering for 39 years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After her first retirement, she took a security course from the WDA and is now working in the Singapore Cruise Centre as a security officer.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If the RRA no longer exists, there is nothing to stop a company from choosing to reimpose or reintroduce an earlier company retirement and re-employment age.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is no doubt that raising the statutory limits further advocates for senior employment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, raising the statutory ages may not translate to more offers of re-employment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The point I am driving at is that these changes ultimately do not address the fundamental problem of a negative perception towards ageing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Misperceptions about older workers and persistent ageist attitudes regrettably still exist within our social fabric, as many employers worry about being stuck with workers who are unable to adapt to remain competitive and become an increasing liability for their business.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, ageing does not have to always be associated with deteriorating health, disempowerment and dependency.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, we can be a society where seniors are empowered, skilled, healthy and active contributors to society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recall in the early 2000s as Singapore was establishing her strength in the biotechnology field, we tapped on the expertise of cancer researcher Yoshiaki Ito, who at age 63 was then facing forced retirement from a university in Japan.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Prof Ito made the move to Singapore in 2002, and along with him, he brought his laboratory members and became a mentor to many other fine researchers who are now part of Singapore's valuable scientific research community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The experience and know-how of seasoned experts like Prof Ito in the early years were crucial building blocks in helping Singapore achieve her status as the regional biotech hub.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The successful integration of senior employees would require a shift in mentality in the workplace that requires a partnership between both employers and senior employees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers have to be willing to take the leap of faith and utilise the current Government schemes to hire and retrain mature workers for the benefit of their companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Likewise, older employees have to be willing and committed to learning and adapting in an ever-changing workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just as we drew on the experience of Mdm Lucy Ho and Prof Ito, we must now look for opportunities to allow Singapore to use the skills of our senior employees despite potential physical or technological limitations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of my fellow union leaders, I would like to put on record that such appeal is not about requiring our workers to work longer, but more so providing the platform for our workers who still want to continue working, not forcing them as it may be perceived.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We believe our older workers can continue earning an income to help meet ongoing living expenses and also strengthen their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC believes that "having a job is the best welfare".

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Workers still have the choice to retire early if they decide to do so.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: If I recall correctly, back in the 2018 Budget debate, NTUC had called for tripartite discussion to review the long-term retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Thereafter, a Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers was convened in May 2018 to review the retirement and re-employment ages and also to consider adjustments to the CPF contribution rates for Older Workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC then engaged close to 500 union leaders across the services, industrial and public sectors over multiple focus group discussions to hear not just the aspirations that workers have but also their concerns.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: After several engagement sessions with leaders, our NTUC representatives, Deputy Secretary Gennerals Heng Chee How and Ms Chiam Hui Fong, and my fellow Central Commitee leaders Brother Phillip and Sister Eileen relayed our collective views to the tripartite workgroup.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The workgroup also studied overseas models of retirement and re-employment to analyse best practices that may aid in their tripartite discussion.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the two factors above, the key to successfully raising the retirement and re-employment ages is creating an inclusive and progressive workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This means that employers proactively discuss and apply a structured career development plan with their older workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This will then allow for training and job redesign to raise productivity and longevity at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers must also be encouraged to provide more re-employment opportunities to retain these experienced workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our workers cannot be terminated on grounds of age, assurance for continued employment up to the statutory re-employment age and not forgetting allowing our employers to redesign jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The role of our fellow workers will have to be reviewed not just with age but also emergence of new technology.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This conversation has to start early for our fellow workers, not limiting to just at age of mid-50s.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The job redesign is critical so that our fellow workers go for training early and as they age, they can be less physical but more productive with use of technology in their course of work.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC can offer our Company Training Committee, or in short CTC, as the platform to train and prepare our workers for re-employment, company by company.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should be using such schemes to provide re-employment opportunities to workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should no longer cite cost of hiring or business needs as an expense of having an experience worker at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There will also be workers who may not want to continue working, and hence that is another beauty of this Bill as it does not enforce workers to work longer, but instead, make employers exercise their responsibility to allow older workers to work longer if they want to.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   Raising age limits under this Act is a measure taken by the Government following several recommendations by the Tripartite Workgroup in 2019.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: As a worker there are some points that I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: First, employers need to conduct early planning for employees by reviewing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should accept that early planning is important to give their workers confidence that they can still contribute and continue to work longer.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I urge employers to make early preparations for their employees and avoid waiting until the employee approaches the retirement age.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should also realise that there are many assistance grants to help them continue employing their workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Avoid focusing too much on the financial cost of retaining your employees, who have been with them from the beginning.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, it is available only for those who wish to continue working for their own reasons.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The unions and the Labour Movement will continue to serve by giving recommendations to employers and the Government only for those workers who wish to continue working.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For those who do not wish to continue working, you can carry on with your retirement plans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my last suggestion for those who opt to retire early.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We know that the amendments to this Act are also related to the Central Provident Fund Act.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This can help ease their financial burden so that they can have a life using the money they had earned when they were working.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): The journey post retirement for a worker always requires some thought.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: From my engagement with retired workers, it is a real stigma to wake up the next day with no employment and wondering what is next.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I remind myself and fellow workers to have a plan early on what to do upon retiring.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We should avoid working actively, if possible, at that age, and spend time catching up with our hobbies and what we may have missed or not able to do so earlier.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would first like to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe and I am confident, that we can do better to improve this figure.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many Singaporeans may still be unaware that making their CPF nominations before their passing will benefit and bring much convenience to their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If a person does not nominate a CPF beneficiary before their own demise, the CPF Board will instead take up to three weeks upon the member's passing to transfer the monies to the Public Trustee Office (PTO) after accounting for transactions such as MediSave deductions for hospital bills.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The PTO will then begin searching for eligible beneficiaries under the law after that.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, can the Ministry share how the amendment will assist in shortening the timeframe for issuing the un-nominated CPF monies to the eligible beneficiaries?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from streamlining and expediting the release of funds for the un-nominated cases, I believe that we can do more to encourage Singaporeans to make their CPF nominations, as that will allow their CPF monies to be distributed to preferred beneficiaries faster and without incurring fees.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the past year, it has been heartening to see the efforts made by the Government in raising awareness in this aspect through short skits featuring the famous Liang Xi Mei character and estate planning workshops organised by various Community Clubs (CCs) with partners such as The Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from these efforts to raise awareness amongst Singaporeans regarding the importance of making CPF nominations, I believe that we should also introduce more tangible benefits to encourage more people to do so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, the Registry of Births and Deaths would notify the CPF Board upon registering a member's death, who would then distribute nominated CPF monies, typically within a month of the member's passing.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the Budget debate earlier this year, I stressed on the importance of releasing the funds expeditiously to the deceased's family and subsequently shared with the CPF Board several anecdotes about my Woodgrove residents who became financially strapped and approached me for assistance when their pillar of support passed away unexpectedly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The nominee can then use this sum to defray the funeral expenses of the deceased.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Next, the CPF Board should target to release the remaining sum to the nominee within seven days after that, which will come just in time to alleviate the family's financial burden.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Typically, the family will, after completing the deceased's funeral and cremation, begin to discuss how to resolve the other estate-related issues pertaining to the deceased, such as the need to expend more costs in engaging a lawyer to apply to the Court for either a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the Homes-Rahe Stress Scale, the death of a loved one, particularly a spouse or parent, is ranked as the most stressful life event, while a divorce is ranked second.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mavis Hetherington, a renowned professor of Psychology, and a leading researcher on the impact of divorce on children's development, once stated that "divorce is not a single event, but a process of transitions affecting the entire family".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Such stressful periods may cause a grieving family member to overlook certain vital matters, such as the remaking of one's CPF nomination.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the series of law awareness talks on estate planning that I have conducted over the years in the community, I have held numerous polls to determine if residents are aware that marriage automatically revokes CPF nominations while divorce does not.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What I learned was that majority of the participants actually knew that marriage automatically revokes CPF nominations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe the credit of such high awareness should go to the dedicated CPF team for diligently sending out written notifications to remind members to make fresh nominations upon their marriage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, most of the residents were surprised to learn that divorce does not automatically revoke the nomination made previously upon their marriage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, some residents had shared their concerns with me about the potential impact on the CPF withdrawal age.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Ministry will continue to reassure CPF members through public education and outreach programmes that this amendment Bill will not change the CPF withdrawal age.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most of us will experience some changes to our health and stamina as we age, and this will affect the intensity and type of work which we can take up for re-employment jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are they working in large corporations or SMEs, local or foreign companies?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many of these are flexible arrangements, part-time and full-time positions?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have a breakdown of the salaries across sectors, occupations and genders?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appreciate the various incentive schemes to encourage companies to hire senior workers such as the Part-time Re-employment Grant and the Senior Worker Early Adopter Grant.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share with the House how has the response been to these programmes so far?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the take-up rates and how many senior workers have benefited from the scheme?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the breakdown of the various sectors and type of companies which had applied for the grants?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry also share updates on the Senior Worker Support Package, which includes the Senior Employment Credit and CPF Transition Offset?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our SMEs employ so many Singaporeans, will there be additional measures to incentivise and support them in our collective effort to keep our senior employees in the workforce?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although we are improving in our drive to be more embracing of older workers, age discrimination continues to persist in some pockets of our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What more can be done to minimise this?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the CPF must provide Singaporeans with a home, old age support, social safety net and protection.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the home ownership policy, Singaporeans can purchase a HDB flat using their CPF.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to providing retirement payouts, CPF also allows residents to have a health insurance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans born after Independence would have a certain amount of CPF fund to help them live through their old age.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is only the older generation that needs the Government's and their families' support to thank them for their efforts in nation building.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is worrying now is the new jobs and industries that have emerged in the new digital age.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Workers in these industries may not have sufficient CPF protection and this will have a far-reaching impact on their retirement security in the future.
