speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I would like to ask the Minister the following questions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, how many people have insufficient minimum retirement deposits in their CPF but have homes that can be monetised with the assistance of Lease Buyback Scheme or other schemes to provide old age security?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, how many people can continue to mortgage HDB flat or private properties to CPF to reach the minimum retirement sum?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fourth, how many people would like to make more CPF deposit or contributions personally but had been rejected?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government consider allowing them to increase their deposits?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fifth, can the Government consider allowing and encouraging donations to third-party CPF accounts to promote a caring society?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sixth, can the Government provide more incentives to mothers' CPF to encourage fertility?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Seventh, can the Government allow children to not ask their parents to refund payments made from their children's CPF when purchasing the HDB flat?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Eighth, can parents allow their children to return education fees paid from their CPF account without any deadline?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will allow CPF to better support Singaporeans at various milestones in their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I have three points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I seek clarification on what will be considered a "significant condition", particularly in relation to auto-immune diseases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, the amended section 77 will provide that the Minister may make regulations, including to provide that a condition is a significant condition only if approved by the Minister and causes disability of a description or to an extent specified by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister confirm that this is not intended to limit all significant conditions to only conditions that cause disability and that the Minister retains broad discretion in determining what conditions are deemed significant conditions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify if serious auto-immune diseases, such as those included under the Chronic Diseases Management Programme (CDMP), will be considered and included as significant conditions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Early withdrawals will ease the burdens on these patients by giving greater liquidity to manage their finances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The increased financial support and flexibility by allowing CPF withdrawals before reaching 55 years of age would be immensely helpful to patients of auto-immune diseases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 25A provides for the reimbursement of reasonable funeral expenses but only to a beneficiary, which would be persons entitled to the CPF monies under various rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In reality, funerals are often arranged expediently upon a person's death.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Loved ones may not know how much CPF funds are available, how much they can use and, indeed, whether they are even beneficiaries at all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may lead to confusion and stress over funeral arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, can the Ministry publish guidelines or a framework to help beneficiaries understand how much funeral expenses will the CPF Public Trustee typically agree to defray?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, can the Ministry expedite the process of informing beneficiaries of their nomination and of the CPF funds available upon a member's death?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three, can the Ministry allow the Public Trustee to reimburse reasonable funeral expenses to a wider class of beneficiaries who have incurred these expenses in good faith?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The death of a loved one is always painful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad this Bill helps soften the blow and I hope the CPF Board will consider my suggestions to take further steps in that direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, I understand that Retirement Account top-ups before November 2008 are returned to the giver when the recipient passes away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The repeal of section 19A changes this and such top ups are no longer returned to the giver.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Members who made top ups before 1 November 2008 would have done so based on their understanding of the rules at that time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Certainty of the rules is important for members to have confidence in our CPF system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By changing the rules and allowing a period for refunds, could this lead to a risk of an exodus of funds from Retirement Accounts as members choose to exercise this option?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will exceptions be made to allow for the prior rules to apply to members with valid reasons?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the Retirement and Re-employment (Amendment) Bill proposes to give our older workers the option to work longer if they choose to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our older workers are treasure troves of experience and our younger workforce has much to learn from them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support this legislative move to allow them the flexibility to work longer should they wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In line with this short Bill, I have three short points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about the minimum retirement age.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 4 of the Act is being amended to constrain the minimum retirement age the Minister can prescribe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, the Minister can prescribe a minimum retirement age of anywhere between 62 and 67 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the new amendment, that range shrinks to between 62 and 65 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify why this range has been reduced?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the Government's current plans are only to raise the minimum retirement age to 65 by 2030.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is the amendment merely to align the new law with the Government's stated plans or is there some other reason for legislatively tying the Minister's hands on this matter?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about differentiated retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill appears to tweak the Minister's power to specify retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill empowers the Minister to prescribe each age to "any class of employees".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is new language not present in the current Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The term "class of employee" is not defined in the Act or in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share whether this change is meant to give the Minister the power to apply a differentiated retirement age and re-employment age to different types of employee?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the Ministry has plans to apply differentiated retirement and re-employment ages to employees in different sectors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last point is close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today's Bill is about senior workers but I would also like to emphasise the importance of senior volunteers, which I know is outside the scope of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we also ensure that there is no discrimination based on age when it comes to volunteerism?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems contradictory to say that someone is not too old to work but is too old to volunteer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Volunteers may start their community involvement only late in their lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is clear that volunteers help to shape our society and country into a better place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They make time, despite their busy schedules and out of the goodness of their heart, to help others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If a senior volunteer's age does not hinder his or her performance in any way, there is no reason why they should be discouraged from continuing their good work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be rewarding them instead for their kindness and desire to give back to our society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of both Bills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is an urgency to review our retirement and re-employment, or R&R, framework to prolong our workforce's longevity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As our seniors live longer and healthier lives, their expectations for living standards will increase.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Raising the R&R ages makes it possible for seniors to stay productive and enjoy greater financial independence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is not uncommon to hear stories of seniors facing difficulties seeking employment in their silver years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must ensure that senior workers are employed in meaningful roles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we need to go beyond numbers to get more insights into the employment landscape for seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share data on the types of professions and roles that seniors are employed in?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How many were successfully re-employed in different sectors from their previous roles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How many were re-employed in the same sector but in different roles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This indirectly pressurised the senior to leave on his own accord.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One Yio Chu Kang resident who was in a managerial position shared that he was asked to relinquish his position so that the company could groom a younger employee to take over.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He thought this was a fair intention but he expected to take on a mentorship role.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Instead, they offered him an entry-level position that was completely unrelated to his previous job scope, skill set and interest.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Feeling insulted, he decided to resign and accept the Employment Assistance Payment (EAP).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was worth noting that his HR manager did not even ask why he rejected the re-employment offer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When re-employment does not work out, getting a new job after 62 can be a tall order due to the misconceived notion that older employees are less productive, amongst other things.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In a February 2020 survey on ageism in the workplace, older workers were stereotypically ranked lower in alertness, ambition, productivity and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They were ranked higher in susceptibility to accidents and resistance to innovation and change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These findings are not true across the board.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may lead seniors to sense that age, by default, limits opportunities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This stiffens their morale and desire to retrain or upskill for career advancement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is interesting to note that a highlight of the MOM Labour Force Report 2020 was the increased number of discouraged workers concentrated in older residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If employers do not change their mindsets, we will lose precious human capital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, both employers and employees need to adjust their mindsets and expectations about re-employment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many companies still use a seniority-based wage system, translating to the belief that wages should rise annually.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Correspondingly, older employees are perceived by employers to be more expensive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Last year, middle-aged and senior residents who have lost their jobs would tell me that they were more than willing to accept a pay cut for their new job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, prospective employers have assumed otherwise, simply because of their age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The mindset that a wage system is necessarily based on age needs to be phased out.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so in this era, where we expect to change careers multiple times in a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When we start a new job in a different industry with fewer responsibilities and relevant skills, we, generally, do not expect to command a similar salary to our previous job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, if a re-employment contract stipulates fewer job responsibilities, it is fair for the salary and benefits to be reduced correspondingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Basically, we should pay an employee based on his worth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, changing someone’s responsibilities without consulting them in advance may result in unnecessary misunderstandings and misconceptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Companies should be upfront and discuss such issues with employees who are due for re-employment and ask about their plans and aspirations moving forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The employee should also be consulted on his or her ability to cope with the demands of the position.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If the company would like to offer the employee a different role, clarifying their intentions would go a long way to reduce misgivings and increase retention rates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There must be a way to implement and promote these conversations for all our employers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The timeline from now until 2030 appears to be unnecessarily prolonged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that the plans to raise the R&R ages will not be affected yet again?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As many companies will look to the Government to take reference, what is the timeline for the Civil Service to implement the raise?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, what is next beyond 70 years old?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will we abolish the retirement age altogether?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A number of countries, including Australia, Canada, the UK and the US, have no mandatory retirement age, with exceptions made for certain professions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This has an impact on the R&R framework.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One such change is the acceptance of flexible working hours and arrangements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some seniors may choose to work less or work from home more, because they want to spend their retirement years with their family or to pursue their own interests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have such workforce changes been taken into account for the R&R framework revision?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The pandemic has posed a threat to senior workers in some ways.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some elderly frontline workers have resigned from their jobs as they were afraid to contract COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have to press on to leverage more on technology to redesign jobs, so that they are less labour-intensive and can be done remotely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share more details about this?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, whether there is a specific timeline for the expected progress and what can employees expect from the redesigned jobs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This worries the lower-income residents, who have less confidence in achieving the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) by 65.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The current recommendations only mentioned the BRS until 2022.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What will it be in 2023 and beyond?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to support Singaporeans to stay in the workforce for as long as they desire.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Yio Chu Kang, I spoke to two residents, both 62 years old and currently employed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She wants to spend more time with her family and her grandchildren and pursue her interest in calligraphy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The additional income from her part-time work would supplement her retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, another resident, Mr B, wants to continue working full-time to accumulate more retirement funds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He is concerned that his employer would not re-employ him on the same terms as before.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He works in an office and does not believe his workload should be reduced or changed because of his age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The difference in attitudes between both seniors is a reminder that there is no one-size-fits-all policy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a progressive society that strives for a senior-friendly workforce, we must avail more employment options so that seniors like Mdm A would not have to choose between working full-time and leaving the workforce completely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Meanwhile, seniors like Mr B, should be able to contribute their fullest potential to the workforce for as long as they wish.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would be facilitated by raising the R&R ages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their fears and anxieties about age discrimination are valid.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must continue to engage employers, with the goal of eradicating ageism.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Employers, too, must communicate with their employees to understand their wishes and to bring out the best in their senior workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to keep the support structures and the assurance that they will receive their CPF payouts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given Singapore’s demographic shifts towards an ageing population and the longer life expectancy of Singaporeans, it is inevitable that many of us will have to continue working for a longer period.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a 9.2% increase from a decade ago.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singapore moves towards a more inclusive workforce that recognises the increased contributions of our older workers, I would like to make three clarifications to ensure that our older employees are safeguarded from unfair employment practices when offered re-employment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On wage adjustment, the tripartite guidelines stated that "Upon re-employment, any wage adjustment should be based on reasonable factors, such as productivity, duties, responsibilities and wage system”.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the tripartite guidelines allow for “the wages to be adjusted down to the level of a younger employee with the requisite experience and competency for the same job", I would like to clarify what are the safeguards in place to prevent employers from disincentivising older employees by overtly reducing their salary, knowing that they need to be re-employed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Continued employment may remain an important channel for older workers to meet their expenditure needs, especially the lower-income earners.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having contributed their years before retirement in an organisation and hoping to be valued for their contributions, older workers should not be expected to be short-changed in re-employment terms and benefits to continue their service with the employer.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to clarify what is the average timeline expected for such conciliation between employers and employees.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that the timeline for these conciliations be short, with amicable solutions reached by both parties, so as not to overtly bring hardship to employees seeking re-employment, especially those who require the job for their livelihood.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, one of the main eligibility criteria for re-employment set out in section 7, subsection(1)(b)(ii) of the Bill is that the employer will assess the employee as "being medically fit to continue working".

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With increased retirement age, there would be a proportional increase of those with multiple chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the higher prevalence of chronic illnesses in an older workforce, I am concerned that irresponsible employers can use it to disadvantage older workers and justify not to offer re-employment on the grounds of medical fitness when they are having common chronic illnesses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our seniors remain important contributors of our economy and society, sharing their wealth of experiences and valuable skillsets while mentoring younger employees.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, legislation is critical to prohibit dismissal on grounds of age and safeguarding their re-employment rights if they wish to continue with their employment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This amendment is an important step in sending out the right signals to the employers that diversity of age at work remains an important driver to increase productivity and allow their business to grow, especially when older employees possess subject-matter expertise and are observed to have lower turnover rates.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Now, on the Central Provident Fund (Amendment) Bill, since its inception in 1955 as a compulsory retirement savings programme, our CPF system has been the bedrock of our social security system, which ensures that the seniors can retire comfortably and be financially independent during their golden years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, CPF Board already allows members to apply for withdrawals if they are certified to have a reduced life expectancy or severe medical conditions that cause members to be permanently unfit for work or lack mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have an encounter with one of my residents, Mdm A, who suffers from a rare and incurable disease characterised by progressive problems with movements and may shorten life expectancy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a mother myself, I can fully understand the intention of Mdm A to support her son through his studies while she is able to, without expectation of repayment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, can the Ministry also clarify if CPF Board will be conducting periodic reviews of the type of specified significant conditions, in order to keep up with newer medical conditions that would be eligible for such withdrawals?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This means that CPF members can make greater voluntary contributions to their MediSave account to prepare them for the "rainy days", where they may face the possibilities of medical emergencies and can use their MediSave to cover a significant portion of medical costs and hospitalisation bills.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I have also come across elderly residents in my constituency who are healthy and raised concerns over the underutilisation of their MediSave balance, requesting if their MediSave funds can be reallocated into their Retirement Account.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It allows a beneficiary of the deceased member to apply to the Public Trustee to become a beneficiary representative.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, I support the amendment Bills.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ageing population narrative is not an unfamiliar one.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our leaders saw it as an eventuality that happens to most developed countries.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Due to a multitude of factors, people are living longer and having fewer children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the differences between Singapore and the rest of the developed world is the speed at which it has happened, along with the other limitations we have, such as, our reliance on our people as a main resource.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The challenges of an ageing population are multi-faceted, spanning from retirement adequacy, healthcare readiness and, with relevance to this Bill, their place in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some do it out of necessity due to financial, familial and a variety of other circumstances too numerous and too personalised for us to paint broad strokes over.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having said that, I lend my support to this Bill in the spirit of protecting the seniors who make up an important part of our workforce and who want to continue to work.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In cultures like Japan, seniority is looked upon with a reverence both in and out of the workplace.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Honorifics are given to the elderly as recognition of the experience that time has given them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it may not be practical to fully adopt the same cultural dynamics, we would do well to remember that both in and out of the workplace, our seniors bring much value, mentorship and expertise.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill keeps our seniors' options open if they want to work and protects against wrongful dismissal, giving our older workers some security and clarity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no magic switch which flicks when you turn 63 or 65.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Your experience continues to be valuable and the skills accumulated over the years remain yours.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My first point is on ensuring that seniors not just have employment, but gainful employment, which is appropriate for them with commensurate salary.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that some seniors may choose to work to keep busy, but there are also seniors who need to continue working due to economic needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The outcome of this shift has to be meaningfully accompanied by job redesign and early career structuring.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, a mature PMET should find opportunities in the same or related roles or roles they are keen on exploring and can be trained for, rather than be shifted to menial or labour-intensive roles, which may be counter-intuitive as he or she hits retirement age.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we continue to raise this age to 65 by 2030, we also need to ensure that our employers actively re-scope job roles and backend processes to unlock the true value of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, this could mean scoping down roles with appropriate salaries, if older workers do not wish or are unable to continue with the same job at the same pace.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than the efforts by the union, which I recognise and applaud, does the Government have any further plans to assist employers and employees on reaching an agreement for fair terms should their role be scoped down?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider providing incentives for companies that actively re-scope roles for seniors and have age-friendly workspaces?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How else can the public sector take the lead in embracing an age-diverse workforce and enhance the culture of workplaces?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can opportunities for older workers be better consolidated and made accessible for this demographic, together with more tailored support, for them to move on into new roles?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While useful for our seniors, I would like to ask if there are any plans for the Government to increase this level of support who do not get re-employed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is already difficult for anyone to look for a new job in this climate, let alone for older workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While our overall re-employment statistics are improving, the rate for our seniors do not seem to be as buoyant.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is lower than the fourth quarter of 2020's 46.7% and the first quarter of 2021's 55.7%.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On an annual basis, the statistics in our second quarter is also lower than nine out of 10 of the previous second quarters.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And considering that the recommended EAP is only for 3.5 months of salary, are there plans for additional support to improve this figure as we navigate our way out of the pandemic?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My second point, the main dispute resolution platform to resolve workplace-related disputes is the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management, or TADM.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: TAFEP and TADM have been very valuable at resolving some of the complaints employees have.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The announcement of future anti-discrimination legislation as well is encouraging.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, while employers cannot forcibly retire elderly workers based on age, it remains that unfair dismissals may happen under the guise of other benchmarks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is the Government considering additional measures to improve the implementation of this policy and how successful has TAFEP been in working with firms to ensure that they no longer practise such ageist company policies?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The final point I wish to make is that, while we all have a role as employees in a society in embracing this shift, the majority of the efforts and costs to ensure all seniors continue to have an important role in the workplace will fall on our employers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are the ones who face not just the monetary responsibility of wages and CPF, but also the responsibility of creating an inclusive workplace designed for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, during this transition period, employers may still find difficulties sustaining long-term employment for seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, there are also members of our Pioneer Generation who still face further difficulties in saving for their retirement, even beyond 70.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The unique socio-cultural context of Singapore makes the task of ensuring our workforce is ready for this move is a difficult one.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened by the Government's move to support the seniors who make up an important part of our workforce and I do have residents to tell me they still feel young at heart and want to continue working.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad we are looking to support those who make this choice.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that our employers, employees and workspaces are also ready to be open to transform in tandem with our policies and appreciate the value of an inclusive and age-diverse workplace.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Deputy Leader, would you like to move that the debate be now adjourned?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Raising the retirement age is essential for Singapore because it benefits our workers for this new economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans can retire when they so choose but raising the retirement age will provide a vast majority of our workforce with a longer runway to contribute to the economy, learn new skills to stay engaged and be able to continue to earn a fair and decent wage to sustain their lives and further build their savings for retirement eventually.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During one of my community engagements with residents, I came across Mr Tony Ho, aged 74, who continues to work as he is willing to put his acquired skills and experience to help companies create value to our economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most recently, he helped to design and execute a new production facility in Tuas for a trading company which wanted to do its own manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He further guided them on how to manufacture these products to be of high quality so as to achieve local market sales.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Tony Ho is a positive example of how our seniors can remain employable, leveraging on their experience and continue to contribute to the larger economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Raising the retirement age will allow our current workforce who are in their early 60s and have optimal capacity and positive attitude, to continue to be a core contributing force for our economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are a part of the experienced workforce we have in the economy, that is, those with more than 15 years of working experience, that forms the core of any company’s competitive talent base – from senior management to professional functions and operations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is an essential reframing of how we need to look at the future workforce composition within a company and across all industries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those in their 40s up to the age of perhaps 65, should be the new bedrock of our competitive economy as we compete higher up the value chain where experience and know-how will be the new value proposition.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Raising the retirement age progressively would allow Singaporeans to work for a longer period instead of being forced to retire due to a perception of what is considered old age.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we proceed to make this happen, there is also a need to ensure that our current social systems and training models support this extension.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I propose two suggestions to allow the benefits of raising the retirement age to be distributed more equitably.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we raise the retirement age progressively, I believe we need to make an adjustment to the age from which CPF contribution rates change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The continuation of an employee's CPF contribution at the same rate, both from employers and themselves, even after 55 years, sends a clear signal that work should be recognised and valued for its intrinsic worth during the most productive periods of an employee.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a shift in mindset throughout the workforce will also prove helpful as we commit to include more middle-aged workers into the bedrock of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cost will always be a concern for employers but the reality today with our demographics is that real value is also being created by those above 55 inside many companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Studies have shown that what matters more in a modern economy is the productivity of teams of workers, rather than individual workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the solution might be to employ a mixture of vigorous young workers and more experienced older workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to take careful steps to bring our society in tandem with our economy and, in doing so, allow employers to reap the benefits of such investments in human capital and employees to feel valued enough to continue innovating and increasing their productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For Singapore’s human capital advantage to be sustained, we need to enable our workers to always remain relevant in this fast-changing economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For our older workers, we need to help them translate their experiences into updated contributions to their job functions and the overall economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Taking a look at ASEAN’s built environment industry, human capacity with the skills and experience remains vital to optimise the integration of advanced digital technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), AI, robotics and cloud computing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, energy specialists go through upskilling courses before they could advise MNCs that are aiming for net zero emissions, or factories looking to measure their Environmental Health and Safety (EHS) leading indicators.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Digital tools should not be seen as the new takeover in making our economy an efficient one, but these tools are to assist our workers who are equipped with upgraded skills to effectively harness these tools.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, Singapore is ranked as one of the countries with the highest life expectancy and we stay healthier for longer even as we grow older.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, like many other developed countries, our population and workforce are ageing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, to meet the intent of the Bill, raising the retirement and the re-employment age must be accompanied by efforts to reduce, and eventually eliminate, the barriers to a truly age-friendly labour market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices, it states, and I quote, “Employers should not stipulate age as a requirement for employment unless there are legal or regulatory requirements which must be stated clearly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Words or phrases that suggest preference for job candidates of a particular age group should also not be used in job advertisements.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, a cursory check on recruitment websites shows a clear age-bias.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On Jobstreet, a job posting for a Quantity Surveyor describes the job highlights as “good career advancement, young and positive work environment.” Just last week, posted on 25 October, a recruitment ad for a part-time horticulturalist states “Looking for part-timers to work in a young and fun environment”.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are just two of many examples that can be found.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond recruitment ads, we would have heard anecdotal stories of how seniors were asked pointed questions about their age at job interviews, leading to the common perception that their age hindered them from proceeding further and securing the job.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During our Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), we would have come across older workers who felt that they were forced to retire as they felt their employers assessed their suitability for the job was based solely on age rather than the objective assessment of their job performances or relevant health conditions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a recent discussion about retirement and re-employment with the residents in Pasir Ris, Ms Judith highlighted the common question of whether it was a case of “have to work” or “want to work” for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Residents Raymond Puah and Charlie Cheong shared that, in addition to protecting and providing opportunities for our senior workers through legislation, the best way to secure re-employment is to upskill and remain relevant in this job market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Raymond Puah even shared that he took the opportunity cost of forgoing overtime pay to upskill and better prepare himself for retirement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Educating employers and legislating Fair Employment Practices will provide opportunities for our seniors who have to work.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, to create a suitable environment for seniors who want to work, we must drive fundamental changes in our HR policies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To better prepare our senior workers, employers must deliberately engage them in a structured career planning conversation well before retirement age.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Job requirements must be clearly defined, along with the relevant skills required such that workers are aware of the prerequisites for future re-employment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would allow workers to add value to the organisation even as they mature.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, given that digital competencies are enablers for re-employment, can the Ministry consider basic digital skills training as a prerequisite for our senior workers in preparation for retirement?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another area to look into is the feasibility and adoption of flexible work arrangements that are already commonly practised around the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most of us start work in our 20s and, as we reach retirement age, we would have spent 40 years or more working.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By then, there would be less financial pressure as our children would be independent and would likely want to spend more time outside of the work environment and enjoy a better quality of life as we head towards full retirement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is understandable that our senior workers want to continue working but with a more flexible work arrangement more suited for their life stage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we encourage companies to consider flexible work arrangements, such as shorter work weeks, part-time employment or even job sharing between two or more persons?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That brings me to my third point on redesigning jobs to leverage on the strengths of our seniors instead of their weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am sure many of us have heard our seniors share their struggles to find employment opportunities outside of roles, such as cleaners, security guards and other labour-intensive roles requiring long work hours.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, they can be physically demanding and require long work hours which do not play to the strengths of our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we come together as a community and provide jobs that leverage on the strengths of our senior workers’ knowledge, experience and wisdom instead?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What have we learnt from the past 20 months where many of us have been able to work productively from anywhere and at any time?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we look into these remote and flexible work arrangements to ensure that our senior workers have more re-employment options?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we employ our senior workers to conduct virtual training classes to share their intrinsic industry knowledge, or provide virtual customer service assistance, virtual consultation or even virtual career coaching?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can even harness technology to redesign jobs for non-PME roles as well, such as helpline operators for carpark gantries, or monitoring lift performance and dispatching teams for lift maintenance, which they can easily do from the comfort and safety of their own homes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must redesign jobs to leverage on the strengths of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will provide better opportunities for re-employment and, at the same time, unlock this potential human capital to support our workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Failure to do so would mean that a significant portion, a third of our workforce, not being properly and purposefully allocated to add value to our economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For this to be successful, we must work together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers must be willing to spend time to restructure jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mature workers must be willing to train while our unions continue to encourage and assist, and Government agencies must provide structural support for this transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a community, how do we encourage and adopt the right mindset to feel responsible in creating these employment opportunities for our senior workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would also like to highlight that although there are many support schemes available, it is difficult to make sense of all the information available on the MOM website.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry consider making it more user-friendly by streamlining the available information to assist the companies?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have spelt out ways to create an age-friendly labour market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Arguably, this takes considerable commitment of time and resources which many of our SMEs can ill afford.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means that SMEs may simply not have sufficient bandwidth to understand the full range of fair employment practices, nor the time and experience to implement career planning and redesign programmes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that SMEs account for an estimated two-thirds of all employment, we need to make the education process easier for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):    This amendment Bill will enable senior citizens who wish to continue working to do so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In view of Singapore's ageing population, the amendments will also enable businesses to benefit from such highly-experienced workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in order to achieve the Bill's objectives, the raising of the retirement and re-employment age must be complemented with anti-age discrimination laws, such as those provided by the TAFEP Guidelines, so that we can protect our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should also change mindset and HR policies, such as having in place flexible work arrangements or career planning, for re-employment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should also strive to redesign jobs that can harness the strengths of our seniors so that we can provide more opportunities for senior workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Speaker, Sir, the proposed amendments enable seniors who wish to continue working to do so.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given our ageing population, it also enables businesses to tap on this experienced pool of workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, to meet the intent of the Bill, raising the retirement and re-employment age must be accompanied by efforts to reduce and, eventually, eliminate the barriers to a truly age-friendly labour market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must expedite the necessary legislation to protect our senior workers and implement fundamental changes in our HR policies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have to look into redesigning jobs to leverage on the strengths of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together, we must look at this challenge holistically and realise that we all have a part to play in this solution.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the amendments in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will give employers time to make the necessary adjustments and preparations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At this stage in our seniors' lives, depending on individual health conditions and personal preferences, it is very likely that most will have some changes to the scope of their work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Re-employment negotiations provide the opportunity for employers and employees to work out new arrangements, including options, such as flexible and part-time work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, for some senior workers who need the incomes, they may not have much room in re-employment negotiations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Older workers with lower education levels are particularly vulnerable to poorer workplace treatment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The fear of losing jobs keep some in unfair arrangements or toxic work environments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these problems may be localised within departments; other issues may be prevalent or systemic within an organisation or a sector.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, due to such difficult conditions, there are workers who resign before reaching their retirement age or forgoing re-employment offers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to find ways to protect and help them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some examples of problematic work conditions include additional duties not within job scopes, volume of work which is difficult to complete during work hours, not providing appropriate or functioning equipment, and refusal to compensate for additional time and expenses incurred in the course of work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Workers may hesitate to seek help from the human resource department or MOM for fear of losing their jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think it is very important for senior workers, especially those who are in lower-paying jobs, to be informed of their rights and to be educated on how to assert their right to fair treatment at work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even more importantly, they need to be assured of support from the Ministry and have confidence in the enforcement of workplace protection legislation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By right, the individual HR departments should handle complaints and feedback, but they may be perceived to be pro-management.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would thus like to suggest that the Ministry consider making it mandatory for companies to hold regular town hall meetings with employees to share feedback and report on follow-up measures.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They must have clear protocols in place to allow whistle-blowers to complain safely and provide multiple avenues for feedback.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to comment on an amendment in the CPF (Amendment) Bill to simplify the process of distributing unnominated monies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I welcome more expedient payouts from the Public Trustee to a beneficiary representative.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It may go some way to help dispel a persistent myth that unnominated monies are taken by the Government.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This issue had been addressed more than once in this House and it was made clear repeatedly that CPF Board and the Public Trustee's Office (PTO) will attempt to locate and contact the next-of-kin so that they can claim the monies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, there is no deadline for them to lay their claims.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: CPF should review its strategy to reach out to the public to address this misunderstanding.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, the monies will be returned to the givers when the recipients die and, in certain circumstances, refunds to the givers are allowed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are some merits to the current arrangement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, top-ups to parents' accounts from children may not be equal and the children who contribute may have some assurance that, in the event of their parents' death, their unused top-ups would be returned to them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not all children are keen to have their top-ups shared among the beneficiaries of their parents' estate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):    Senior workers who need the incomes do not have much leverage during re-employment negotiations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Older workers with lower-education levels may be more likely to encounter poorer workplace treatment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As they are afraid of losing their jobs, some employees endure unfair arrangements or poor working conditions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, some senior workers are unwilling to continue accepting such difficult conditions and choose to resign before reaching the retirement age or forgo re-employment opportunities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to find ways to protect and assist them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, CPF top-ups, upon the death of the recipients or, in certain circumstances, can be returned to the givers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, top-ups to parents’ accounts from children may not be equal.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not all people are willing to let their top-ups become part of their parents' estate to be shared among all beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I worry that with this amendment, there will be fewer people who are willing to top up their parents' CPF accounts, and elderly women will be more affected.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most of them have less savings and longer lifespans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): With this, I support both Bills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Projected inflation in a post-COVID-19 world has caused much anxiety.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many people are getting increasingly worried that they will not have enough savings to support retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can take heart that our CPF is an acclaimed retirement income system that is a constant work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government is always reviewing and refining it to ensure it stays relevant with the times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The latest Mercer CFA Institute Global Pension Index report graded our CPF system as being on par with countries like Finland, Sweden and Switzerland.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The grading meant that it has a sound structure with many good features but some areas for improvement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe our Government is always working towards closing the gaps.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The beneficiary representative would then distribute the monies to the beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would apply if the total amount of the member’s CPF monies does not exceed the specified limit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does this policy serve to benefit the family of members who did not name any nominees?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would be welcomed as I have residents who are still waiting for years to resolve the distribution of CPF monies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry also clarify how this process will be simplified and sped up?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Who is eligible to be a beneficiary representative and what is the specified limit?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With that, I understand that there is still some amount of hesitancy towards nominating beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The topic of death remains a heavy one to broach and some CPF members tend to take it for granted that there will always be a seamless transfer of CPF monies to their families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would take this opportunity to remind all that life is unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Arranging how our assets will be distributed would bring great peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also urge the Government to remind members in simple terms, if possible, and make it easier for them to nominate their beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As far as I am aware, refunds were never supposed to be given for accepted top-ups under the Retirement Sum Topping-Up scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And this is especially so because members who make CPF top-ups get personal income tax relief based on their contributions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This policy is clearly stated on the CPF website.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, can the Ministry clarify what were some circumstances under which refunds were approved, if any?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, I note with interest that the amendments also seek to provide greater flexibility and efficiency in the administration of the Act by providing for certain matters to be prescribed by subsidiary legislation, or to be determined by the Board or the Minister, instead of being stated in the Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that the payment of interest would cease upon notification of a member’s demise in respect of the amount outstanding to the credit of the member that has not been transferred to the general monies of the CPF.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If it takes a significant length of time, like a year or so, that is quite a significant amount of interest that is lost.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, how can transfer be expedited with minimal loss of interest?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, who makes the decision if there are rights issues, or opts to sell the shares because of mandatory purchase by a majority owner?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They also appreciate that it is a safe and effective way to grow one’s retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was a member of the CPF Advisory Panel from 2014 to 2016 and one of the recommendations was that every CPF member should be encouraged to have his or her own CPF LIFE plan with incentives to top-up the CPF Accounts for families with lower balances.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially important for housewives who are relying on their husband's CPF LIFE payouts, as women tend to outlive their husbands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Panel had proposed then that members be allowed to transfer their CPF savings above what they require for Basic Retirement Sum to their spouses' Special or Retirement Accounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this way, each spouse would benefit from the extra interest for lower CPF balances and have their own lifelong income from CPF LIFE.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I am glad to see that amidst the uncertainties of the pandemic, there was a 40% increase in the number of members who made voluntary top-ups of their own or for their loved ones’ CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a testament to the trust that Singaporeans have in the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the other end of the spectrum, I have residents who hesitate to top up their CPF because they are afraid if they need the money, they will not be able to get it out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These tend to be the people who have lower incomes, who would benefit most from the additional top-ups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The difficulty to tap on large sums of CPF savings in times of need, such as a major illness, remains a significant pain point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope the Government will take this into consideration and introduce greater flexibility into the system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the Government’s plans, moving forth, to improve in this area?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides CPF, are we looking at other options, like tax-approved group corporate retirement plans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to increase the CPF withdrawal age?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Netherlands, which is among the top ranking on the index, is raising its pensions withdrawal age from 65 to 67 years old in 2024.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I believe the broad thrust of the speeches made by Members has been supportive of a more expedited process to disburse un-nominated CPF funds but some questions have arisen as to the process and how we safeguard the integrity of the disbursements, which I understand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I will deal with the questions raised by Ms Ng Ling Ling, Ms Hany Soh, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Ms He Ting Ru, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Joan Pereira on this point.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling and some Members have raised concerns that there could be a lack of recourse in cases where the beneficiary representative, whom I shall call "BR", does not exercise fairness in distributing the deceased’s un-nominated funds or unreasonably withhold the funds from beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling has raised some questions concerning the application process: how to identify the BR; how the Public Trustee intends to ensure the welfare of the remaining beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat sought clarifications on whether the policy will serve to benefit the family of members who did not name any nominees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: He also asked who is eligible to be a BR and what is the specified limit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked about the BR process: whether it could simplify and speed up the distribution of un-nominated CPF funds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar asked about the recourse that next-of-kin may have in the BR approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And to be clear, by beneficiaries, I refer here to those who are eligible for and entitled to the deceased CPF members’ un-nominated monies under the Intestate Succession Act for non-Muslims and the Administration of the Muslim Law Act for Muslims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The BR approach will, therefore, benefit these eligible beneficiaries of the deceased CPF member.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a comparator, the BR approach, in this case, that we have introduced is not an entirely new concept.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members might recall the “proper claimant” approach adopted by CPF Board which applies to cases where the nominee passes away after the deceased member has passed away and before the CPF funds could be distributed to the nominee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CPF Board pays out the CPF monies due to the nominee to a “proper claimant” who is a party that claims to be entitled to the monies or assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the concept and process are similar and, in some ways, modelled on the "proper claimant" approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have considered the operation of that scheme and also thought about the issues of potential abuse that could be mitigated and addressed in this current BR scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we have introduced various safeguards to ensure that the beneficiaries’ rights and interests remain protected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is not pre-identified from the list of eligible beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Rather, letters are sent out to the deceased CPF member’s next-of-kin and the individuals who reported the death, to invite them to submit a claim.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Upon receipt of the letter, the eligible beneficiaries of the deceased can come together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can then, amongst themselves, identify and choose a representative.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If they can all agree on that, that is the one representative that will come forward, on behalf of this pool, to make the claim and receive the payment from PTO.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the eligible beneficiaries, however, cannot agree on a BR, or do not wish to appoint one, or is unable to come to an agreement as to how to distribute the un-nominated CPF funds amongst the eligible beneficiaries, then the current claim process will apply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we will default back to the current position.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will be a little bit more complicated, more forms need to be filled up, more information is to be provided to PTO but it will safeguard the process where there might be some disagreement between the beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The PTO will also carry out the following steps to safeguard the rights and interests of the eligible beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Additionally, upon receiving the information, PTO will also undertake independent checks to verify the eligible beneficiaries’ details provided by the BR against available existing records.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, do a bit of due diligence to cross-check the information, to cross-verify the information provided by the BR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If there are discrepancies, the PTO might require further clarifications or further information before disbursing the funds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Ms Mariam Jaafar’s question, in cases of dispute over the nomination of the BR, the eligible beneficiaries may seek recourse by informing the PTO of the dispute.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If that happens, the PTO will not proceed with the application for the BR to distribute the un-nominated sums.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will instead discuss with the eligible beneficiaries and see whether some consensus or an agreement can be reached.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Failing which, again, we default back to the current standard process, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If despite these steps taken by the PTO to weed out these cases, there might be situations where the BR receives the un-nominated CPF funds before the disputes are surfaced and, subsequently, there are disputes over how it is disbursed or the manner in which it is done, the eligible beneficiaries can seek recourse against the BR directly under the law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the new proposed section 25A(7) of the Bill makes it clear that any recourse that any person might have against the BR for any amounts paid out by the PTO to the BR are not affected even after payment of the un-nominated sums by the PTO to the BR.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides the PTO’s actions taken to safeguard the rights and interests of the beneficiaries, the framework is in-built with a safeguard to only apply to cases where the deceased member’s un-nominated sums do not exceed this sum.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This specified limit, in our view, strikes a balance between expediency in the disbursement of the funds and safeguarding of the beneficiaries’ rights and interests, particularly in the context of larger estates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Ms He Ting Ru's question, the specified limit can be reviewed and adjusted in the future, if necessary, to allow more people to benefit from the BR approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we suggest we let this run for some time and iron out any rough spots before we look at adjustments subsequently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With the various safeguards put in place for this new BR approach, eligible beneficiaries, in appropriate cases, who have consented to the BR receiving and distributing un-nominated sums, can benefit from this simplified and expedient new process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Hany Soh asked how the BR approach will assist in simplifying and speeding up the process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Apart from what I have mentioned earlier, let me highlight that the BR approach only requires the BR to provide proof that he or she is the eligible beneficiary with all the beneficiaries’ details, including his or her own.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The BR need not submit proof of eligibility of all the other eligible beneficiaries, so this cuts down part of the administrative time and effort.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The BR approach relieves the other beneficiaries from administrative inconvenience.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: By and large, in the majority of these cases, there is no disagreement, as I have mentioned, and, in such a situation, particularly amongst family members, the facilitation of the disbursements can be much faster.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Once the PTO receives confirmations, as I have outlined earlier, from all the eligible beneficiaries and the verifications are done, the application can be approved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar asked about the efforts made to contact and facilitate the disbursements of CPF monies of a deceased member to Singaporean family members who might be overseas, especially in light of the current continued travel restrictions in the ongoing pandemic.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As the PTO oversees the distribution of un-nominated CPF sums, I will address this point only on un-nominated sums, as far as the PTO is concerned, where the member did not make a nomination.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such cases, the PTO will take steps to reach out to the deceased member’s next-of-kin, regardless of whether they are residing in Singapore or overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Using the next-of-kin’s last available address registered with the National Registration Office, the PTO will write to the next-of-kin using that address.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Obviously, efficiency is subject to whether the address is accurate, whether it has been updated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the overseas address is not registered, then PTO will rely on the member's next-of-kin to provide the office with any available alternative information.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Deceased CPF members’ next-of-kin who are residing overseas can also choose to contact PTO to enquire about the deceased CPF member’s un-nominated CPF monies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The process is entirely digital, the deceased CPF members’ next-of-kin who are residing overseas can submit their application to the PTO via the PTO’s online application form, together with any necessary supporting documents to evince or substantiate their position, including and proving their familial relationship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, generally, the answer to Ms Jaafar's question is that we will take proactive steps within reasonable information to identify these beneficiaries overseas and we will also try and facilitate in as easy as possible the distribution and disbursement of sums to them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested publishing guidelines or frameworks to help beneficiaries understand how much funeral expenses the Public Trustee typically agrees to defray.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question, relevant information on PTO’s reimbursement of funeral expenses is already currently available on PTO’s website.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Louis Ng also suggested allowing the Public Trustee to reimburse reasonable funeral expenses to a wider class of beneficiaries who might have incurred these expenses in good faith.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such a requirement serves to protect the interests of the deceased CPF member’s eligible beneficiaries when the cost of the funeral expenses is being claimed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
