text: This also alleviates the risk of the PTO making payment to a claimant whom the eligible beneficiaries might well dispute the entitlement of the payment to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On her first point, to the extent possible, PTO will obviously try to facilitate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think it is in everyone's interest, including PTO, to try and find a solution and find consensus on a BR, so that the process can be simplified and expeditious.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Failing that, the Member knows that there are a number of options for mediation for the parties to come to a consensus.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not always standard and not always easy for every such situation because the reasons for the conflict may differ from case to case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But to the extent possible, PTO will try to facilitate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There were many points raised, reflecting the wide spectrum of views and the common interest we share in supporting our senior workers and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Allow me to make a few general points before I address specific comments from Members on the Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We constantly and continually review our policies and we will take Members’ suggestions into consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The speeches have touched on the need to adjust our culture and our mindsets, both as a society and as businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members also touched on important questions, which the Tripartite Workgroup on Older Workers had deliberated on extensively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In doing so, they considered the many perspectives which emerged from their public engagements, before arriving at their very balanced recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the issue of whether a statutory retirement age is still needed, as highlighted by Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Sylvia Lim and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, the Workgroup had considered this very carefully.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It looked at the experiences of other countries and found that countries without the equivalent of a statutory retirement age do not necessarily have better employment rates for senior workers, despite some of them having anti-discrimination legislation already in place.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some progressive employers may take the initiative to abolish their internal retirement age and allow workers to work for as long as they wish, and we wholeheartedly applaud them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But as Mr Heng Chee How emphasised, the statutory retirement and re-employment age is still important as a floor and safeguard against employers who might not be as progressive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The continued relevance of this approach is borne out by facts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore’s average effective retirement age has risen faster than the OECD average.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These considerations, and the data that support them, are captured in the Workgroup’s comprehensive report.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I encourage all Members to study the report.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On pace of implementation, the tripartite partners negotiated this very carefully before arriving at a consensus.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The timing of future adjustments will depend on prevailing economic conditions, but the resolve to stay the course is clear.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why the range of retirement age that the Manpower Minister can prescribe in the law is being reduced from 62 to 67 years to 62 to 65 years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, before 2012, the concept of re-employment had not been introduced yet, so the only lever we had was the retirement age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But since then, we have seen how the concept of retirement age and re-employment age works well in combination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The proposed legislative amendments thus fully reflect the tripartite consensus on this roadmap.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is our model: tripartite consultation with stakeholders, tripartite consensus and then tripartite implementation, with legal changes to reflect the plan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do not rule out future changes to our approach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This model of constructive tripartism will ensure that we are able to adapt and respond to such needs in the decades to come.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Ng Ling Ling, Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Mariam Jaafar have spoken on the need to ensure that employers fulfil their re-employment obligations and that re-employment offers are fair.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Tripartite partners have agreed upon a reasonable set of guidelines, laying out employers’ and employees’ responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will just highlight a few guidelines that are more relevant to the situations that Members have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, early communication and discussion are critical to ensure that re-employment offers are reasonable to both parties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, on the issue of medical fitness, they should offer re-employment to eligible workers who are medically fit to perform any job within the company, not just the existing job role.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers are also advised to presume that their senior employees are medically fit, unless there are clear reasons to believe otherwise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Ms Ng Ling Ling’s concern, having chronic conditions alone cannot be used to justify denial of re-employment, if it does not affect their ability to perform the job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The re-employment framework is designed to balance the need to enable senior workers to continue working, while giving employers sufficient flexibility so that businesses can remain nimble and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we must strike a very careful balance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Indeed, different individuals have different needs and expectations as they approach retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While some may want to stay on in their current roles, others may desire a job role with reduced work intensity or see themselves trying out new roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is why the tripartite partners have agreed that employers and employees should be given the flexibility to negotiate adjustments to the job roles, wages and benefits, as long as they are reasonable and based on factors like productivity, responsibilities, skills and the employer’s wage system.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Notwithstanding this, the vast majority of re-employed workers continue on their existing contract or a new contract in the same job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If an employer has considered all available re-employment options within the organisation and is unable to identify a suitable job for the senior worker, the firm may offer him or her an Employment Assistance Payment, or EAP, as a last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Patrick Tay’s queries about the sufficiency of the EAP amount, a fine balance was struck by the Tripartite Workgroup.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If the EAP is too high, it may deter employers from hiring jobseekers who are approaching retirement age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If the EAP is too low, employers may too readily offer to pay the EAP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is in tandem with the growth in general wage levels.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling also asked about the success rate for conciliation of re-employment disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: After more than 10 years of implementation, we find that the majority of cases are often resolved expeditiously at mediation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This leaves a few cases that need to be surfaced to the Employment Claims Tribunal (ECT) for adjudication.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Janet Ang, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Henry Kwek, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Nadia Samdin also highlighted ageism and discriminatory employment practices as a concern.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We agree that ageism and workplace discrimination of any form have no place in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am glad that Members’ speeches in this House over the past two days also recognise that legislation is not a silver bullet nor a panacea.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In this regard, I agree with Mr Heng Chee How, who has very wisely pointed out that strengthening the employability of our senior workers cannot start only when they are near retirement age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There is a need to invest in retraining and employment facilitation not only for our senior workers, but also for the future cohorts of senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Mr Patrick Tay has highlighted, employers play an instrumental role in this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we are committed to providing the necessary assistance, including funding support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Ms Nadia Samdin’s query on the extension of the Senior Employment Credit beyond 2022, we will also study it and update in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, I have already spoken extensively on the various ways that the Government is supporting upskilling and employment opportunities for senior workers in my response to several Parliamentary Questions last month.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, today, I will just highlight the critical roles that our tripartite partners NTUC and SNEF play in this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Company Training Committees, or CTCs, established by NTUC early this year, are making their impact felt.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The CTCs bring together the employers, HR and employee representatives to identify gaps and opportunities and develop the necessary training plans to align a company’s workforce to its business transformation roadmap.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This ensures that our senior workers’ training needs are correctly identified, to enable them to contribute productively for many more years to come.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As highlighted by Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Abdul Samad and Ms Janet Ang, it is also important for companies to have structured career planning conversations with their employees, especially for those in their 40s or 50s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows training needs and suitable job roles to be identified early.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employees will also be more motivated to pick up new skills if they have a clearer picture of how they fit into their companies’ future plans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are working with both SNEF and NTUC to encourage more employers to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are many other areas where the tripartite partners have been working closely on, including encouraging job redesign and flexible working arrangements, which Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Henry Kwek, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Patrick Tay, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Ms Nadia Samdin have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We encourage the tripartite partners to do more and we will continue to give our fullest support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we make these legislative changes today, we will also continue to work with the tripartite partners to study best practices and review our framework where necessary to ensure its continued relevance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned by Mr Shawn Huang and Ms Yeo Wan Ling, it is also important for our workers to adopt a lifelong learning mindset.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Continuing Education and Training, or CET, is just as important as pre-employment training (PET), as a means for our workers to upgrade their skills, remain relevant and keep pace with global trends and developments.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On CPF withdrawals, Mr Abdul Samad and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim suggested to allow members to start their CPF monthly payouts earlier, while on the other hand, Mr Saktiandi Supaat suggested to start later.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, let me reassure everyone that the Government has not suggested changing the Payout Eligibility Age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Payout Eligibility Age, or PEA, is not linked to the retirement or re-employment age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The current PEA of 65 strikes a balance between timely access to retirement income and providing a sufficient runway for members to build up savings for retirement, especially as Singaporeans are expected to live longer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members continue to have the option to defer the payouts for higher monthly payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members will also continue to have the flexibility to make lump sum withdrawals from age 55, years before they start their monthly CPF payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The banker friend that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has, and I believe is likely to be as successful as Assoc Prof Lim himself, will be able to withdraw amounts well above the retirement sum at 55.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes the $5,000 that he can withdraw unconditionally and the amounts in excess of his Basic Retirement Sum, given that he will likely own a property.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Similarly, the amendments to section 15 of the CPF Act are only intended to simplify it, and not alter the underlying policies and operational flexibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Louis Ng, Ms Ng Ling Ling, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Miss Cheryl Chan and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked what constitutes a “significant condition” in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are now collectively referred to as “significant conditions”.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill provides for these same grounds to be prescribed in the Regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, there are no changes to the qualifying rules for early CPF withdrawal.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To Ms He Ting Ru's point, I would like to clarify that members with reduced life expectancy will, indeed, be able to benefit from the automatic disbursement of Ordinary and Special Account monies that I mentioned in my speech yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On Ms Ng Ling Ling’s suggestion to allow waiver of loan repayments under the CPF Education Loan Scheme for such members, I am happy to confirm that CPF Board already does so today on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In simplifying the CPF system, CPF Board will also ensure that implementation is smooth for its members.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the top-up rules and the position of givers, CPF Board will take into account Mr Louis Ng and Ms Joan Pereira’s suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I do believe that Singaporeans top up their loved ones’ CPF accounts out of the generosity of their hearts and to help boost their loved ones' retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The objective is to simplify things for members, in response to feedback that the existing rules can be confusing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some top-ups are refunded to givers when their recipients exit the CPF system, while, as Mr Saktiandi Supaat observed, other top-ups are treated as gifts to recipients and not refunded, including cash top-ups made after 2008.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Hany Soh spoke about facilitating the disbursement of nominated monies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nonetheless, CPF Board has plans to continuously streamline the disbursement process for nominated CPF monies and I thank Ms Hany Soh for her suggestion on this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond simplifying policies and streamlining processes, CPF Board will also continue to strengthen its public education and outreach efforts, as Mr Melvin Yong and Miss Cheryl Chan highlighted.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will include educating members on the benefits of CPF top-ups to self and loved ones; nudging members to make nominations; making clear that nominations, like wills, are, indeed, revoked upon marriage; and clarifying the treatment of CPF monies upon members' passing, as alluded to by Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Hany Soh and Ms He Ting Ru, as well as Ms Joan Pereira respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also explore Ms Hany Soh's suggestion to send notifications to divorcees to prompt them to review their nominations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Several Members of the House have provided feedback on policies which are not quite within the scope of today's Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, Ms Ng Ling Ling and Miss Cheryl Chan on the allocation of monies across CPF accounts, Mr Yip Hon Weng on the Basic Retirement Sum, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Gan Thiam Poh on housing issues, Mr Patrick Tay and Miss Cheryl Chan on self-employed persons, as well as Mr Saktiandi Supaat on tax-approved group corporate retirement plans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will take all these into consideration as we review our policies from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is in tandem with the first increase in CPF contribution rates for senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In closing, I would like to thank Members of the House for their support of the Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The two Bills will help our members in three main ways: first, by providing members the flexibility to work longer if they wish to; second, by making it easier for members to build up their retirement nest egg; and third, just as important, by making it easier for members to receive their retirement payouts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Together, the Bills will help our members better prepare for and enjoy their retirement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have a clarification for the Minister regarding the statutory retirement age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, he mentioned that the consensus among the tripartite partners was that this was still necessary on the statute books as it serves as a floor to protect workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My question is that most, if not all, employment contracts, as I have mentioned in my speech, do have a termination clause where either the employer or the employee can give notice of a short period, one to two months, to stop the employment relationship and no reasons need to be given.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And if notice is not sufficient, payment in lieu can be made in accordance with that clause.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, would we not agree that, actually, that clause can be exercised at any age of the employee?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that extent, my question is how far does having a statutory retirement age in that sense undermine the operation of that clause which is in the contract?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, I am aware of the fact that many companies, especially those hiring, those with senior management employees, for instance, have this clause which puts many, many workers on fixed employment contract terms.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We should look at it from different angles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Ms Sylvia Lim's point about many of these contracts being fixed-term contracts, the tripartite committee on workplace fairness will also look into the legislation covering age discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I have a clarification with regard to the eligibility payout at 65.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Has MOM done a study on how many of those actually choose to retire early, maybe because of age or they just want to retire early?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, can they actually ask for their CPF payouts to be at an earlier age compared to 65?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: That was the main gist of me requesting for the Ministry to explore the possibility if someone decides to retire before the legislative age because they want to do something personal.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To them, it is their money and they are also requesting whether they can get part of the share.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If his property is pledged – and I believe the majority of Singaporeans today would have a property and it is pledged to the CPF – he can withdraw not just the $5,000 at the age of 55, he can also withdraw a sum higher than the $5,000 from his Special Account and his Ordinary Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If he has the Full Retirement Sum (FRS) set aside, which is double that of the BRS – I think it is now $186,000; because it is $93,000 multiplied by two – if he does not have his property pledged to CPF, he can withdraw, again the minimum $5,000, and amounts in his Special Account and also the Ordinary Account.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the Payout Eligibility Age (PEA) set at 65 is really reserved for the amount, the BRS or the FRS, in his Retirement Account to stream out the monthly payout starting from 65.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For those who were born on or after 1958, this will go into CPF LIFE and it will be streamed out as an insurance annuity that will be paid out for life every month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nowhere in any of the changes that we are proposing today, which I hope that Members will support, would change any of the dynamics whatsoever.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The members can still withdraw their money from age 55 onwards, but subject to those conditions that are already in existence today.
